description: Researched, licence-verified catalogue of free Godot resources. NOT a record of what is vendored — see THIRD_PARTY_LICENSES.md for that.
method: Parallel research agents searched GitHub/GitLab and the web, then fetched each project LICENSE file directly to confirm the licence; a second skeptical pass re-verified clonability, Godot 4 compatibility and size for everything proposed for vendoring.

resources.name: controller_icons (rsubtil) — Godot addon with CC0 Xelu glyphs + runtime device detection
resources.license_evidence: curl https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rsubtil/controller_icons/master/LICENSE -> 'MIT License / Copyright (c) 2023 Ricardo Subtil / ...to use, copy, modify, merge, publish, distribute, sublicense, and/or sell'. README §License: 'The addon is licensed under the MIT license. The controller assets are Xelu's FREE Controllers & Keyboard PROMPTS, made by Nicolae (XELU) Berbece and under Creative Commons 0 (CC0). Some extra icons were created and contributed to this addon, also on the same CC0 license'. README also states the addon logo derives from Godot's icon.svg which is CC-BY-4.0.
resources.asset_license_note: CODE AND ART VERIFIED SEPARATELY: code MIT, art CC0 — both clean. Only caveat: the addon's own logo derives from the Godot logo (CC-BY-4.0); exclude that single file or record the attribution. A second LICENSE exists at addons/controller_icons/LICENSE.
resources.why: Bridges the art and the UX: gives you the Xelu CC0 glyph set (401 PNGs) AND the code that picks the right glyph per connected device, so prompts update live when a player switches from keyboard to gamepad. That is the accessibility/platform-UX work this sweep is responsible for, and it is genre-independent. Complements the Kenney prompts (different visual style — Xelu is flatter/darker, Kenney is rounded/lighter), so vendoring both gives the team a style choice.
resources.teaches: How to swap input glyphs at runtime based on the last-used device, and how to bind a glyph to an InputMap action rather than a hardcoded key — the correct architecture for input UX, worth reading even if you use different art.
resources.notes: Measured by real clone: 6 MB, 401 PNG, 2 SVG. Overlaps slightly with the parallel sweep's 'input remapping' remit — included here because the CC0 GLYPH ART is this sweep's deliverable; flag the code half to the other sweep so it is not double-vendored.
resources.verified_license: MIT ('Copyright (c) 2023 Ricardo Subtil') at master/LICENSE, with a second identical MIT copy at addons/controller_icons/LICENSE
resources.fetch_command: git clone --filter=blob:none --no-checkout --depth 1 --no-tags -b master https://github.com/rsubtil/controller_icons third_party/controller_icons && cd third_party/controller_icons && git sparse-checkout set --no-cone 'addons/controller_icons' 'LICENSE' 'README.md' && git checkout
resources.attribution_required: yes, conservatively — retain the MIT notice, which is what the repo actually grants over the glyphs
resources.rejection_reason: Default branch is master. plugin.cfg confirms Godot 4 addon (Controller Icons v3.1.8, 'automatic icon remapping'). Clone 10MB / 6MB worktree; addons/controller_icons is 5MB of which assets/ is 5MB. Vendoring is fine — just correct the licence metadata from 'MIT + CC0' to 'MIT throughout (art not separately dedicated in-repo)'.

resources.name: Godot State Charts
resources.license_evidence: raw main/LICENSE: "MIT License / Copyright (c) 2023 Jan Thomä"
resources.asset_license_note: No third-party art of consequence; icon.svg is the project's own under MIT.
resources.why: The single best-in-class FSM/HSM addon for Godot 4 and the biggest missing piece in our vendored set — beehave gives us behaviour trees but nothing gives us hierarchical/parallel state machines. Pure GDScript (no binary, no build step), editor-integrated with a live in-editor debugger, atomic/compound/parallel/history states, delayed and automatic transitions, and expression guards. Genre-agnostic: it is the right backbone for a player controller, an enemy, a UI flow, or a turn phase machine, so it holds optionality open whichever game we pick.
resources.teaches: Statecharts (Harel) done idiomatically in Godot: states are nodes, transitions are resources, guards/events instead of ad-hoc bools.
resources.notes: Root repo is 33MB mostly from raw_assets/ and the example project; the addon itself is small. It bundles addons/gut for its own tests — exclude that, we already have gdUnit4 via beehave. Ships an optional C# API (godot-state-charts.csproj) we can ignore on a GDScript project.

resources.name: Input Helper (nathanhoad)
resources.license_evidence: raw main/LICENSE: "MIT License\n\nCopyright (c) 2022-present Nathan Hoad"
resources.asset_license_note: Code only.
resources.why: The lightweight alternative to G.U.I.D.E — 1MB, no architecture to learn, covers device hot-swap + remapping + rumble, which is 80% of what a small team needs. Good default for a jam-scale or undecided project.
resources.teaches: Minimal autoload that reports the active input device, distinguishes joypad families, gets/sets action bindings for a remapping UI, and wraps joypad rumble.
resources.notes: Pairs cleanly with rsubtil/controller_icons for the glyph half.
resources.fetch_command: git clone --depth 1 --no-tags -b main https://github.com/nathanhoad/godot_input_helper third_party/godot_input_helper
resources.rejection_reason: CLEAN. config/features=PackedStringArray("4.4", "C#", "Forward Plus"); plugin.cfg version 4.7.0, i.e. actively tracking current Godot. 1MB, ships docs/, examples/ and tests/. SCOPE NOTE FOR THE PARENT: the brief assigns 'input remapping' to the PARALLEL sweep ('general gameplay addons … input remapping'), and this addon's core features are device hot-swap + remapping + rumble. Check with the other sweep before committing, or you may end up with both this and G.U.I.D.E. Same author as the Dialogue Manager entry, so house style is consistent if you keep it.

resources.name: GLoot
resources.license_evidence: raw master/LICENSE: "MIT License / Copyright (c) 2022 Peter Kish"
resources.why: The reference inventory system for Godot 4 and the strongest candidate in a category we have nothing for. It covers the whole ladder — plain, stack-limited, weight-limited, and Diablo-style 2D grid inventories — with matching UI controls and built-in serialisation, plus an editor for the item prototype database. Because it is model/view-split it is genuinely genre-agnostic: an RPG uses the grid view, a survival game uses weight constraints, an FPS uses a flat 4-slot inventory over the same core. Two megabytes, pure GDScript.
resources.teaches: Modelling items as prototypes plus per-instance properties, and separating inventory *model* (capacity, stacking, grid constraints) from inventory *view* (drag-and-drop Control nodes).
resources.notes: Active dev on dev_v3.0.0; vendor master. Overlaps slightly with Pandora (item *definitions*) — GLoot owns runtime containers, Pandora owns authoring a large typed item catalogue; they compose.

resources.name: Panku Console
resources.license_evidence: raw master/LICENSE: "The MIT License (MIT) / Copyright (c) 2024 Feo (k2kra) Wu"
resources.why: This is the biggest force-multiplier for a team whose game is undecided: a drop-in console that evaluates arbitrary GDScript at runtime, registers custom commands, shows live-updating expression monitors, an FPS/system monitor, an interactive scene/node inspector, and a log window with export. Prototyping speed on an unknown genre is dominated by iteration loops, and a REPL against the live scene tree collapses those loops. Desktop-only concerns (windowed sub-panels, keyboard-driven) suit our target exactly.
resources.teaches: Exposing an in-game REPL over GDScript's Expression class, plus building live-editable inspector widgets for tuning values without a rebuild.
resources.notes: Only addons/panku_console is needed; the rest is the demo project and docs site. Gate it behind an export feature tag or OS.is_debug_build() so it does not ship in the Steam release.

resources.name: Godot Safe Resource Loader
resources.license_evidence: raw master/LICENSE: "MIT License / Copyright (c) 2023 Jan Thomä"
resources.why: The obvious, ergonomic way to write a Godot save file is ResourceSaver/ResourceLoader on a custom Resource — and doing that naively is a remote-code-execution hole, because a tampered save in user:// can carry a script that runs on load. Any save system we build (or any Steam Workshop / mod / cloud-save story) needs this guard. It is a small, focused, MIT drop-in from the same author as godot-statecharts, and it is the piece that makes the Resource-based save approach actually safe to ship on Steam.
resources.teaches: That Godot's ResourceLoader will execute embedded GDScript in a .tres/.res file, and how to strip script payloads before deserialising anything that came from disk, a mod folder, or the network.
resources.notes: Exclude the bundled addons/gdUnit4 (tests only). This is a *component* of a save system, not a save system — pair it with our own SaveManager and with Maaack's persistence (already vendored).

resources.name: Sky3D
resources.license_evidence: raw.githubusercontent.com/TokisanGames/Sky3D/main/LICENSE.txt -> 'MIT License / Copyright (c) 2023-2025 Cory Petkovsek and Contributors / Copyright (c) 2021 J. Cuéllar'
resources.why: Closes the sky/day-night gap with the ecosystem's best answer (864 stars, MIT, actively developed). Same authors as the already-vendored Terrain3D, so the two are designed to sit in one project — that pairing is worth more than either alone. Atmospheric scattering, dynamic sun/moon, cloud layers, fog integration.
resources.teaches: A production-grade time-of-day system: how sun/moon transforms, atmospheric scattering parameters and cloud layers are driven from a single normalised time value.
resources.notes: Addon lives entirely in addons/sky_3d (12 MB); demo/ and screenshots/ can be dropped if size matters.

resources.name: Pandora
resources.license_evidence: raw main/LICENSE: "MIT License / Copyright (c) 2023 bitbrain & contributors."
resources.why: Every genre we might pick needs a catalogue of typed things — items, enemies, buildings, cards, upgrades — and Godot's built-in answer (a folder of hand-made Resources) does not scale or support inheritance. Pandora gives a first-class editor dock, category hierarchies with property inheritance, typed properties, and generated IDs, which is the difference between a designer-editable game and a programmer-bottlenecked one. Same author as beehave (already vendored), so quality and maintenance are known-good.
resources.teaches: Data-driven game content: an in-editor typed entity database with category inheritance, so designers author items/enemies/spells without touching .tres files by hand.
resources.notes: Stores content in a single data.pandora file; pairs with GLoot (runtime containers) and with Godot's built-in Resource system. Note the repo carries GdUnit4 test config — tests only.

resources.name: Godot Debug Menu
resources.license_evidence: raw master/LICENSE.md: "# MIT License / Copyright © 2023-present Hugo Locurcio and contributors"
resources.why: A three-key-press overlay showing frametime graphs, 1%/0.1% lows, CPU vs GPU time, and full hardware/driver identification. For a Steam + Steam Deck target this is the primary tool for answering 'is this GPU-bound on Deck?' and for making user bug reports actionable. Written by Calinou (a Godot maintainer), one megabyte, no dependencies, and it is deliberately shippable — many games leave it in behind a hotkey.
resources.teaches: What to actually measure on a shipping build: frametime percentiles (not average FPS), CPU/GPU time split, VRAM, and the exact GPU/driver/OS string to attach to a bug report.
resources.notes: Complements Panku Console rather than duplicating it: Panku is a REPL/inspector, this is a hardened perf HUD. Keep both.

resources.name: Debug Draw 3D
resources.license_evidence: root master/LICENSE is a pointer to addons/debug_draw_3d/LICENSE; that file reads "MIT License / Copyright (c) 2026 DmitriySalnikov"
resources.asset_license_note: Code MIT; no shipped art.
resources.why: Godot has no built-in immediate-mode debug drawing, and the moment we touch 3D AI, pathfinding, raycasts, or physics we will be blind without it. This is the mature, widely used GDExtension answer — thousands of primitives per frame, in-world text, graphs, and a release-build no-op path. Highly relevant because the genre is undecided: if we go 3D at all this becomes load-bearing on day one, and if we stay 2D it costs us nothing to have indexed.
resources.teaches: Immediate-mode debug geometry: drawing lines/boxes/spheres/frustums/text from any script for one frame, and how to keep it zero-cost in release builds.
resources.notes: GDExtension with prebuilt binaries distributed via GitHub Releases rather than the repo, so vendoring the source alone is not enough — record the release download step (Windows + Linux .so/.dll) alongside it. Verify the binary set covers linux x86_64 for Steam Deck.

resources.name: Questify
resources.license_evidence: raw main/LICENSE: "MIT License / Copyright (c) 2024 TheWalruzz"
resources.why: The strongest permissive quest addon: a graph editor for authoring quests, an autoload manager that tracks active/completed state, condition-driven objective completion, and serialisation for saves. Nothing in our vendored set does quests — godot-open-rpg has an RPG scaffold but not a general quest graph. Two megabytes, pure GDScript, and genre-portable (a survival game's crafting milestones are the same data shape as an RPG's fetch quest).
resources.teaches: Modelling quests as a graph of objectives with conditions and rewards, tracked by a manager autoload with serialisable state.
resources.notes: Direct alternative to shomykohai/quest-system; Questify is graph-authored (designer-friendly), quest-system is code-authored (engineer-friendly). Vendor both only if we want the comparison; otherwise Questify first.

resources.name: Juicee
resources.license_evidence: raw main/LICENSE: "MIT License / Copyright (c) 2026 kelpekk | frogy"
resources.why: Game feel is the difference between a prototype that reads as fun and one that does not, and it is the fastest lever available before the genre is even decided. Juicee is a Feel-style (Unity FEEL-inspired) effects library with a visual graph editor, inspector-authored effects, and a one-liner runtime API covering screenshake, hitstop/freeze-frames, camera punch, and property tweening. MIT, 5MB, actively developed in 2026.
resources.teaches: Composing game-feel as authored, reusable effect assets (a graph of shake/flash/hitstop/tween curves) triggered by a one-line call, rather than as scattered ad-hoc Tweens.
resources.notes: Overlaps deliberately with Shaker (below) and with phantom-camera (vendored, which has its own noise/shake emitters). Recommended split: phantom-camera for camera *framing* and its built-in noise, Juicee for authored multi-part feedback bursts.

resources.name: ThemeGen
resources.license_evidence: raw master/LICENSE.md: "MIT License / Copyright (c) 2024 Inspiaaa"
resources.why: Godot's Theme resource is powerful but authored entirely through the inspector, which makes any real design system painful to build and nearly impossible to refactor — you cannot share a colour between twenty StyleBoxes without hand-editing twenty StyleBoxes. ThemeGen makes the theme a generated artefact from readable code with reusable variables and composable style functions. For an undecided genre this is exactly the right investment: it makes the UI layer cheap to restyle when the art direction lands.
resources.teaches: Themes as code: define colour/spacing tokens once in GDScript, derive StyleBoxes and per-control overrides from them, and regenerate the .tres Theme — so a palette change is a one-line edit instead of hundreds of inspector clicks.
resources.notes: Editor/authoring-time tool — the output is a plain Theme resource, so there is no runtime dependency on the addon in the shipped game.

resources.name: Resources as Sheets (resources_spreadsheet_view)
resources.license_evidence: raw master/LICENSE.md: "# MIT License / Copyright 2022 Gennady \"Don Tnowe\" Krupenyov"
resources.why: Balancing and localisation are both bulk-edit problems, and Godot's inspector is a one-object-at-a-time tool. This turns a directory of .tres files into an editable grid with paste-from-Excel and CSV import/export, which makes stat balancing, loot tables, and translation-string tables tractable for a small team. It is the pragmatic half of the localisation workflow ask: Godot's built-in CSV/PO translation import is already good, and what is actually missing is a comfortable editor for the string table — this provides it.
resources.teaches: Editing a folder of Resources as a spreadsheet — multi-row select, column-wise edits, copy/paste from a real spreadsheet, and CSV round-tripping.
resources.notes: Editor-only, no runtime footprint. Complements Pandora: Pandora is a typed entity DB with inheritance, this is a fast grid over plain Resources/CSV. Discovered via TakinGodotTemplate's addon set.

resources.name: Godot Shader Warmup
resources.license_evidence: raw main/LICENSE: "MIT License / Copyright (c) 2026 Mattia Domizio"
resources.why: Shader-compilation stutter is the number one performance complaint in shipped Godot 4 games and it is worst on the exact hardware we are targeting — Steam Deck's RDNA2 driver plus Vulkan pipeline creation. This addon pre-warms shaders at startup and interoperates with the engine's own shader baker, with measured results published in the repo. It is a ship-blocker-class problem solved by a small MIT addon, which makes it high value even though the genre is undecided (every genre stutters).
resources.teaches: Pre-compiling pipeline state objects at startup/loading time so first-encounter shader compilation does not produce a visible frame spike mid-gameplay.
resources.notes: Includes a gdext/ native component — confirm prebuilt Windows and Linux x86_64 binaries are present or buildable before relying on it. Cross-check against Godot 4.7's built-in shader baker; the addon may be redundant for some pipelines and complementary for others. Repo carries a report.pdf with benchmarks worth reading.

resources.name: GPUTrail
resources.license_evidence: raw.githubusercontent.com/celyk/GPUTrail/main/LICENSE -> 'MIT License / Copyright (c) 2023 celyk'
resources.why: Trails and beams are absent from the repo and are a staple of melee, projectile and vehicle feel across many genres. This is the modern Godot 4 GPU implementation (293 stars, MIT, 1 MB) and is the technically interesting one — the older Godot-Trail-System and proton_trail rebuild geometry on the CPU each frame.
resources.teaches: Doing trail geometry entirely on the GPU — history stored in a texture and expanded in the vertex shader — instead of the usual CPU Line2D/ImmediateMesh rebuild.

resources.name: Scene Manager
resources.license_evidence: raw godot-4.x/LICENSE: "The MIT License (MIT) / Copyright © 2021 GlassBrick" (note: the default `main` branch has no root LICENSE; the Godot 4 branch does)
resources.why: Cheap, high-visibility polish: a library of fade/wipe/pattern transitions triggered with a single call, plus transition-covered scene swaps. Maaack's Game Template (vendored) already ships a loading screen with a progress bar for heavy scenes; this covers the other half — fast, stylish transitions between light scenes and menus — with a much lower ceremony API. Small, MIT, genre-agnostic.
resources.teaches: One-line scene changes with a shader-driven transition, and where to put the async load so the transition covers the hitch.
resources.notes: MUST clone branch godot-4.x, not the default branch. Overlap check: if we standardise on Maaack's scene loader, keep this only for the transition shaders.

resources.name: Shaker
resources.license_evidence: raw main/LICENSE: "MIT License / Copyright (c) 2024 Enes Kaplan"
resources.why: A focused, well-scoped shake system with emitters that can drive *any* property (position, rotation, FOV, light energy, UI offset) in both 2D and 3D, using noise rather than random jitter so it reads smooth. Narrower than Juicee but better at the one thing, and the arbitrary-property targeting is genuinely useful outside cameras. Indexed as the alternative to pick if Juicee's graph editor feels heavy.
resources.teaches: Noise-driven shake as a generic property modulator — shake any property on any node in 2D or 3D, not just a camera transform.
resources.notes: Repo is 108MB almost entirely demo scenes and their assets — vendor only addons/shaker (small). Do NOT vendor the demo: its asset licences are unverified.

resources.name: Godot Doctor
resources.license_evidence: raw main/LICENSE: "MIT License / Copyright (c) 2025 codevogel (Kamiel de Visser)"
resources.why: The single most common Godot bug class is a null @export that nobody wired up in the inspector, and it always surfaces at runtime, often in the one scene nobody retested. Godot Doctor validates scenes and resources at edit time (including PackedScene type validation) and reports problems in a dock. For an agent-assisted codebase this is disproportionately valuable: it converts a class of silent scene-wiring mistakes into immediate, machine-readable errors.
resources.teaches: Declaring per-export validation rules on a script so unwired @export references and misconfigured scenes are reported in the editor instead of crashing at runtime.
resources.notes: Ships a C# project alongside GDScript; only addons/godot_doctor is needed.

resources.name: Signal Lens
resources.license_evidence: raw main/LICENSE: "MIT License / Copyright (c) 2025 Yann Lemos"
resources.why: Signals are Godot's primary decoupling mechanism and its primary source of invisible bugs — a connection that was never made, or one made twice, produces silence rather than an error. Signal Lens shows, for any node in the live remote scene tree, its full connection graph and real-time emissions. One megabyte, zero runtime cost, and it directly attacks the hardest-to-debug failure mode in any Godot codebase regardless of genre.
resources.teaches: Reading a running game's event graph: which signals a node exposes, what is connected to them, and when they actually fire.
resources.notes: Editor debugger plugin; pairs with Panku Console (state) and Godot Debug Menu (performance) to give three orthogonal debug views.

resources.name: Health / HitBox / HurtBox components
resources.license_evidence: raw main/LICENSE: "MIT License / Copyright (c) 2023 David Clutter"
resources.asset_license_note: Repo contains assets/ and images/ for its example scenes — verify or exclude those; vendor addons/ + example only if the example art is confirmed permissive.
resources.why: Nearly every action-shaped genre needs the same four primitives — a health pool, something that deals damage, something that receives it, and a hitscan variant — and teams rebuild them badly every time. This gives all four as reusable nodes for 2D *and* 3D with damage/healing signals, which is the right shape for an undecided genre: the same components serve a 2D platformer and a 3D shooter. Small, MIT, with an example project and tutorials.
resources.teaches: Composition-over-inheritance combat: health, hitbox, hurtbox and hitscan as independent nodes that any entity can mount, in both 2D and 3D.
resources.notes: Check the abstract-classes / 4.4-abstract branches for the current Godot 4.4+ API before wiring in.

resources.name: GodotVisualShader-Extras
resources.license_evidence: raw.githubusercontent.com/paddy-exe/GodotVisualShader-Extras/v4.x/LICENSE.md -> 'MIT License / Copyright (c) 2022 Patrick (FlameLizard)'
resources.why: The natural complement to the already-vendored ShaderV: where ShaderV is 2D noise/blur/shape/colour, this adds spatial-oriented nodes (fresnel, vertex animation, screen-space helpers, dissolve/outline building blocks). Vendoring both means the VisualShader editor covers 2D and 3D, which today it does not.
resources.teaches: How to register custom VisualShaderNode types from GDScript — the extension point ShaderV also uses, shown on a different and largely non-overlapping node set.
resources.notes: Clone with -b v4.x.

resources.name: boujie_water_shader
resources.license_evidence: raw.githubusercontent.com/Chrisknyfe/boujie_water_shader/main/LICENSE.md -> '# MIT License / Copyright (c) 2023-present Zach Bernal and contributors'
resources.asset_license_note: MIT throughout; example/ is 49 MB of demo scene art. Vendor addons/ only (4 MB measured).
resources.godot_version: 4.1, Mobile renderer in demo (shader itself is renderer-agnostic)
resources.why: A stylised lake/river water with depth-based shoreline foam and caustics — a different look from GodotSSRWater, so the two together give the team a choice rather than a single locked art direction. Still actively maintained. Full clone measured 63 MB; vendor addons/ only.
resources.teaches: Shore-foam via depth-texture comparison and normal-map flow scrolling — the stylised counterpart to GodotSSRWater's physically-motivated approach.

resources.name: QuestSystem
resources.license_evidence: raw main/LICENSE: "MIT License / Copyright (c) 2023-present Shomy"
resources.why: A deliberately small, extensible quest manager where a quest is a Resource subclass you write in code. Worth having indexed as the low-ceremony alternative to Questify for a team that would rather express quest logic in GDScript than in a graph — for many genres (roguelike run objectives, survival milestones) that is the better fit. Also has a C# branch.
resources.teaches: A minimal, subclass-driven quest contract (Quest resource with start/update/complete hooks) that stays out of your way — the opposite design philosophy to a graph editor.
resources.notes: Repo measures 120MB because it vendors addons/gdUnit4 and docs assets; only addons/quest_system is wanted (a few hundred KB). Lower priority than Questify — vendor sparse or link-only depending on tree budget.

resources.name: LimboAI
resources.license_evidence: raw master/LICENSE.md: "Copyright (c) 2023-2025 Serhii Snitsaruk and the LimboAI contributors. Permission is hereby granted, free of charge..." (verbatim MIT). raw master/LOGO_LICENSE.md: "LimboAI Logo ... licensed under the Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International license (CC BY 4.0)"
resources.asset_license_note: Logo is CC-BY-4.0 — allowed under policy if attribution is recorded, but simply not shipping it is cleaner.
resources.why: The most complete AI package for Godot 4: BTs *and* HSMs, a dedicated editor, a visual runtime debugger, and native C++ performance. Indexed rather than vendored because we already have beehave (behaviour trees, GDScript) and are vendoring godot-statecharts (HSM, GDScript), which covers the same ground with no binaries. LimboAI's advantage appears only at scale — hundreds of AI agents where GDScript tick cost matters — so it is the documented escalation path if profiling demands it.
resources.teaches: Combining behaviour trees with hierarchical state machines under one editor and one visual runtime debugger — the architecture most shipped AI actually uses.
resources.notes: C++ GDExtension: the repo is source only, prebuilt binaries come from GitHub Releases, and adopting it means owning a binary update cadence per Godot version. That cost is why it loses to godot-statecharts + beehave for a genre-undecided team. Its CC-BY logo is branding only; do not ship the logo, or attribute it if we do.

resources.name: godot-sqlite
resources.license_evidence: raw master/LICENSE.md: "MIT License / Copyright (c) 2019-2026 Piet Bronders & Jeroen De Geeter"
resources.why: The right persistence answer for the subset of genres where the save file is a *world*, not a snapshot: colony sims, city builders, grand strategy, long-run survival. A JSON or Resource save rewrites everything on every autosave; SQLite writes deltas transactionally and survives a crash mid-save. Actively maintained since 2019 (copyright line runs to 2026), MIT, and it is the standard answer in the ecosystem. Link-only because it is genre-contingent — if we pick an arcade or action game it is dead weight.
resources.teaches: When a game's state outgrows a single serialised blob — incremental writes, queries over world state, and crash-safe transactional saves.
resources.notes: GDExtension with a vendored godot-cpp; binaries come from Releases. SQLite itself is public domain, so no licence conflict. Revisit and vendor the moment we choose a simulation-shaped genre.

resources.name: godot_atmosphere_shader
resources.license_evidence: raw.githubusercontent.com/Zylann/godot_atmosphere_shader/master/LICENSE.md -> 'Atmosphere shader for Godot Engine / Copyright (c) 2021 Marc Gilleron / Permission is hereby granted, free of charge, to any person obtaining a copy' (MIT text)
resources.why: Covers the one sky case Sky3D structurally cannot: an atmosphere seen from space, on a curved planet. Narrow but decisive if a space/planetary direction is picked, 2 MB, MIT, from Zylann (author of godot_voxel), and 16 shader files make it a solid scattering reference regardless.
resources.teaches: Volumetric atmospheric scattering rendered from outside the volume — the planetary case Sky3D's ground-level sky dome cannot express.
resources.notes: Only worth activating for space/planetary concepts; keep indexed but low priority otherwise.

resources.name: Godot Palette Swap Shader
resources.license_evidence: raw.githubusercontent.com/KoBeWi/Godot-Palette-Swap-Shader/master/LICENSE.txt -> 'MIT License / Copyright (c) 2025 KoBeWi'
resources.why: Palette swap is the standard way a 2D game gets team colours, enemy variants and damage flashes from one sprite sheet, and nothing vendored does it. From KoBeWi, a Godot engine maintainer, so the code quality and 4.x correctness are dependable. MIT, 4 MB.
resources.teaches: Index-map palette swapping with animation support — the technique behind per-player recolours and flashing damage states without duplicating sprite art.

resources.name: PlatformerController2D (Ev01)
resources.license_evidence: raw .../main/LICENSE -> 'MIT License\n\nCopyright (c) 2021 Ev01'
resources.asset_license_note: Code only; the art used by the demo lives on a separate 'assets' branch, so the main branch carries no third-party art.
resources.godot_version: 4.0 (config_version=5, config/features=PackedStringArray("4.0")); runs on 4.x, a 3.4 branch also exists
resources.why: Tiny (1MB), MIT, and it is exactly the 'movement feel' checklist from the brief expressed as tunable exported properties. Even if the team picks a different genre, the height/time-to-peak parameterisation is the standard trick worth copying into any 2D character.
resources.teaches: Textbook platformer game-feel in one exported-variable-driven class: coyote time, jump buffering, variable jump height via jump-cut, separate rising/falling gravity, apex hang, acceleration/friction split for ground vs air, and double jump — all tuned from the Inspector in 'jump height / time to peak' units rather than raw gravity numbers.

resources.name: Nakama Godot client SDK
resources.license_evidence: raw.githubusercontent.com/heroiclabs/nakama-godot/master/LICENSE -> "Apache License / Version 2.0, January 2004 / http://www.apache.org/licenses/"
resources.asset_license_note: Code Apache-2.0 (note: Apache-2.0 requires you to keep the NOTICE/LICENSE and state changes; it is patent-granting and MIT-compatible). No art assets.
resources.godot_version: Godot 4 branch is master (a separate godot-3 branch exists); addon path addons/com.heroiclabs.nakama
resources.last_activity: 2026-07-22 ("Add Nakama.get_device_id() for stable and secure device authentication (#231)")
resources.why: Best breadth-per-byte item in the whole domain: 2 MB of GDScript that unlocks accounts, cloud saves, leaderboards, matchmaking, parties, chat, friends AND realtime/authoritative multiplayer against a genuinely open-source Apache-2.0 server you can self-host. Because the *entire* stack is Apache-2.0 there is no vendor lock and no licence risk. Actively maintained (last month). This is the single item that most reduces 'we picked genre X, now we need a backend' risk, since it serves a leaderboard-only puzzle game and an authoritative RPG equally well.
resources.teaches: Client-side patterns for session tokens/refresh, storage objects with ownership and permissions, leaderboard/tournament writes, the matchmaker ticket flow, and realtime socket + authoritative match RPCs.
resources.notes: DECISION NOTE: Nakama is a *backend*, not netcode. Its relayed matches are fine for turn-based/card/strategy; its authoritative matches run your Go/TS/Lua logic server-side at a fixed tick and are fine for slower real-time games; but it does not do client-side prediction or rollback. The winning combination for an action game is netfox (prediction/rollback in-engine) + Nakama (identity, matchmaking, persistence). Verify the addon against 4.7 on vendoring — Heroic Labs tracks Godot releases but with a lag.
resources.verified_license: Apache-2.0 (full 203-line Apache License Version 2.0 text at master/LICENSE)

resources.attribution_required: no beyond Apache-2.0 obligations: retain LICENSE and NOTICE, and state changes if you modify the files
resources.rejection_reason: CLAIM VERIFIED and the size claim was if anything pessimistic — 2MB clone, 1MB worktree. Godot 4.4 (project.godot features "4.4"), default branch master. One correction to the rationale: this repo is the CLIENT SDK only. The 'genuinely open-source Apache-2.0 server you can self-host' is a separate project (heroiclabs/nakama) which I did NOT verify here, so the no-vendor-lock argument rests on an unchecked premise. Vendoring the client is cheap and safe regardless.

PowerKey targets exactly that gap. Indexed as the answer to 'our localisation has variables in it' rather than as a general localisation replacement.

Indexed rather than vendored because it is an architectural commitment — adopting Nodot means adopting its worldview across the project, which is exactly the kind of lock-in a genre-undecided team should avoid. Worth knowing it exists if we later want a batteries-included component base.

Only vendor because the cost is negligible.

resources.name: RhythmNotifier (michaelgundlach)
resources.license_evidence: raw .../main/LICENSE -> 'MIT License\n\nCopyright (c) 2024 Michael Gundlach'
resources.asset_license_note: Code only; no bundled audio.
resources.godot_version: Godot 4 addon (no root project.godot; distributed as an addon node class)
resources.why: Rhythm is one of the named genres and this is the licence-clean, Godot-4, actively maintained answer to its core problem in 1MB. It is also quietly useful in non-rhythm games — beat-synced enemy spawns or UI pulses work in any genre, which is exactly the optionality an undecided team wants.
resources.teaches: Beat-accurate audio synchronisation: a node that emits custom signals on a specified beat or every N beats, driven off the actual AudioStreamPlayer playback position rather than a timer — which is the whole reason naive rhythm games drift.
resources.notes: Solves timing, not charts or input scoring — pair with rhythm-game-utilities for chart formats. Best thing to steal: deriving beat position from playback position + latency, never from accumulated delta.

resources.license_evidence: Cloned main branch; LICENSE.txt -> "Copyright (c) 2021-2022 David Snopek / Permission is hereby granted, free of charge, to any person obtaining a copy of this software and associated documentation files (the \"Software\"), to deal in the Software without restriction..." (MIT body).

resources.godot_version: main branch: project.godot config/features=PackedStringArray("4.6"); plugin.cfg version=1.0.0. (The older godot-4 branch is stale at 4.1/alpha7 — clone main, NOT godot-4.)

resources.why: The canonical GGPO-lineage rollback addon for Godot, now at a real 1.0 on the main branch and updated for Godot 4.6 in mid-2026 — the netcode used to ship Retro Tank Party. Small (2 MB), MIT, pure GDScript. Where netfox does client-server prediction, this does peer-to-peer deterministic rollback, which is the correct architecture for tight 2-4 player action/fighting games where every frame of input latency is felt. Also ships genuinely rare tooling: a desync debugger and log inspector.
resources.teaches: GGPO-style rollback: SyncManager, per-node _save_state/_load_state/_network_process, input serialization, hash-based desync detection, SyncReplay and a log inspector for diffing two peers' state frame by frame.
resources.notes: DECISION NOTE — this is the expensive fork in the road. Rollback requires a FULLY DETERMINISTIC simulation: no floats where you can avoid them, no engine physics (Godot's physics is not deterministic across machines), no un-seeded randomness, no reliance on node order. Budget for rewriting your movement/physics against a fixed-point library (see sg-physics-2d) before committing. Choose rollback only for small-session, latency-critical, deterministic games. For anything with many entities, an open world, a dedicated server, or non-deterministic physics, use netfox instead. IMPORTANT: the GitHub name SnopekGames/godot-rollback-netcode does NOT exist — the project lives on GitLab and GitLab clones fine here (gitlab raw over curl returns 404, so verify licences by cloning).
resources.verified_license: MIT (same repo as the Snopek entry above; LICENSE.txt, 'Copyright (c) 2021-2022 David Snopek')
resources.rejection_reason: REJECT AS DUPLICATE — this is byte-for-byte the same repository as 'Godot Rollback Netcode (Snopek)' earlier in the same submitted list (identical URL https://gitlab.com/snopek-games/godot-rollback-netcode). The researcher submitted it twice under two different rationales (netcode vs deterministic simulation/replay). The resource is good and should be vendored ONCE using the fetch command given in the earlier entry; the index can carry both rationales as tags against that single vendored copy. Rejecting here purely to prevent a double checkout, not on merit or licence.

resources.name: godot webrtc-native (WebRTC MultiplayerPeer)
resources.license_evidence: raw.githubusercontent.com/godotengine/webrtc-native/master/LICENSE -> "MIT License / Copyright (c) 2018 Godot Engine"
resources.asset_license_note: Code MIT. Bundles thirdparty/ (libdatachannel and friends) — those carry their own permissive licences (MPL-2.0/BSD family) and must be checked before static-linking into a shipped binary. No art.
resources.godot_version: Official Godot org GDExtension, tracks current Godot 4.x; use the tagged release binaries rather than building.
resources.why: Non-negotiable if a browser build is ever on the table. Browsers cannot open raw UDP sockets, so ENetMultiplayerPeer simply does not exist on web export — your only two options are WebSocketMultiplayerPeer (TCP, head-of-line blocking, fine for turn-based/card/strategy) and WebRTCMultiplayerPeer (unreliable/unordered datagrams, the only web-viable transport for action games). On web the WebRTC classes come from the browser via Godot's JS bridge; on desktop they only exist if you add this GDExtension. Maintained by the Godot org itself, actively developed this month, tiny.
resources.teaches: How WebRTCMultiplayerPeer/WebRTCPeerConnection map onto Godot's high-level MultiplayerAPI, and the signalling handshake (offer/answer/ICE) you must supply yourself.
resources.notes: DECISION NOTE: WebRTC needs a signalling server and usually a STUN/TURN server; the protocol does not give you matchmaking. The already-vendored third_party/godot-demo-projects/networking/webrtc_signaling demo is the reference signalling implementation — pair the two. For a desktop-only game, plain ENet is simpler and you can skip this. Vendor the source, but ship the official release binaries; building it pulls a large libdatachannel/openssl thirdparty tree.

It will very likely still run on 4.7 (pure GDScript, no editor plugin surface), but 'best-documented permissive Godot 4 GOAP' should be indexed as 'Godot 4.0-era, expect to touch it'. The complementarity argument against the already-vendored beehave (behaviour trees answer 'what does the NPC do', GOAP answers 'how does it reach an unscripted goal') is sound and worth keeping in the index tags. Index it so that the moment anyone says "rollback" the determinism cost is visible in the same hop.

resources.notes: DECISION NOTE: dormant since April 2024 and it is a C++ GDExtension, so you must compile it against godot-cpp for 4.7 and re-test. Only pull this in if you have already committed to rollback + 2D. Do not vendor speculatively — 10 MB of C++ you may never build.

GodotSteam — the maintained alternative — has moved entirely off GitHub to Codeberg, which is blocked in this sandbox, so this is the vendorable option.
resources.teaches: How to swap ENetMultiplayerPeer for a platform transport with zero changes to your RPC/MultiplayerSynchronizer code — the clean demonstration that Godot's high-level multiplayer is transport-agnostic. The demo branch is the official multiplayer_bomber demo with the peer swapped in.

Treat as a frozen reference implementation, not a maintained dependency: read it to learn the MultiplayerPeer contract, but if you actually ship on Steam, plan on GodotSteam's own MultiplayerPeer (Codeberg, MIT) which is the maintained path. Note the design difference the README documents: this uses Steam *Sockets* (connection-oriented, ENet-like, no lobby required); GodotSteam's peer uses Steam *Messages* (connectionless, requires Steam lobbies). Steam integration also hard-locks distribution to Steam — do not build it into your core loop if itch/console/mobile are still possible.

resources.name: DungeonGenerator (ollelogdahl)

resources.asset_license_note: Public domain, no obligations.

resources.verified_license: Unlicense / public domain ('This is free and unencumbered software released into the public domain.')
resources.rejection_reason: DOWNGRADED from vendor-sparse to link-only — this is GODOT 3, not Godot 4, and the item is filed as if it were current. Evidence: project.godot has config_version=4 (Godot 4 projects are config_version=5, as every other item here shows), and the GDScript is unambiguously 1.0: 'onready var parent = $"../"', 'parent.connect("dungeonGenerated", self, "_on_dungeonGeneration")' (the three-arg Godot 3 connect signature), and 'func _process(delta)' with Godot-3 Input/CanvasLayer patterns. None of this runs on 4.7 without a full rewrite. Only one branch exists (master, ed01f82) so there is no Godot 4 branch to fall back to. Second problem: a 32MB DungeonGenerator.exe is committed at the repo root, making a naive clone 47MB / 33MB worktree for what is a few hundred lines of logic. The Unlicense does mean an engineer can freely read and re-implement the BSP approach — which is exactly what link-only supports. Redundant with Gaea for actual use.

resources.verified_license: MIT ('Copyright (c) 2019 Marco F') — present on both the master ref and the Main branch
resources.fetch_command: git clone --filter=blob:none --no-checkout --depth 1 --no-tags -b Main https://github.com/MarcoFazioRandom/Virtual-Joystick-Godot third_party/virtual-joystick && cd third_party/virtual-joystick && git sparse-checkout set --no-cone 'addons' 'LICENSE' 'README.md' && git checkout

Anyone who fetches this repo without '-b Main' — including any tool that defaults to master — silently gets an unusable Godot 3 addon. The Main branch IS Godot 4: config_version=5, features PackedStringArray("4.2", "GL Compatibility"), and virtual_joystick.gd uses 'class_name VirtualJoystick', '@export var pressed_color', '@export_range(...)'. Vendor from Main only. 2MB clone / 1MB worktree.

resources.name: Kenyoni Godot Addons (Licenses, AspectRatioResizeContainer, Custom Theme Overrides, GLogging, Icon Explorer, QR Code)

resources.why: Two of these addons solve problems we provably have. `licenses` manages third-party copyright/licence entries with categories, descriptions and links and renders them in-game — and this repository is a vendored library of third-party code and CC0/CC-BY assets, so a maintained in-game attribution screen is a compliance requirement, not a nicety (our THIRD_PARTY_LICENSES.md needs a runtime counterpart before we ship on Steam). `aspect_ratio_resize_container` is the responsive-layout helper the brief asks for: it swaps child layout by aspect ratio, which is precisely the Steam Deck (1280x800, 16:10) vs desktop 16:9/21:9 problem. `glogging` gives structured logging, `custom_theme_overrides` extends theming, and `icon_explorer` speeds up editor work.
resources.teaches: How to render a legally adequate third-party licence/credits screen from structured data, and how to make Control layouts respond to aspect ratio rather than to fixed resolutions.
resources.notes: Ten addons in one repo, 6MB total — vendor whole and cherry-pick at install time. Contains addons/kenyoni (shared base) which the others depend on. Branches godot/4.4 and godot/4.5 exist; confirm which tracks 4.7 before wiring in.

It covers the brief's 'static typing, signals, autoloads, node vs resource, performance' bullet in one vendored drop, and it is the only permissively-licensed text I found that addresses 4.7 specifically. 1.26 MB for 21 dense documents is an outstanding density-to-size ratio.

Vendor it as a strong prior, and make the index note that the 4.7 class reference wins on any conflict. Prefer VENDORED over distilled: the per-skill granularity is the value, and condensing it would destroy the routing structure.

Skills cross-reference each other explicitly ("Related skills: …"), which is exactly the one-hop routing behaviour the index is trying to create. Genre-neutral: an agent can pull ability-system for an action game or inventory-system for an RPG from the same vendored tree once the genre is chosen.
resources.teaches: 55 skills / 249 markdown files, each a SKILL.md plus a references/ folder. Directly on-brief: gdscript-patterns (static typing, await/coroutines, lambdas, match, export annotations, inner classes), gdscript-advanced, event-bus, dependency-injection, component-system, godot-code-review, godot-optimization, godot-testing, and export-pipeline whose references include ci-cd-github-actions.md and distribution-itch-steam.md.

THE SIZE IS NOT THE SPRITES — it is audio: 250 .ogg/.wav files totalling 76MB (single largest file is medieval-fantasy/sounds/forest-ambience.wav at 5.0MB, uncompressed). The pixel art everyone actually wants is only ~20MB across all eight packs. Two honest options: (a) take the 8 folders as listed (93MB) and treat the CC0 music as a genuine prize — CC0 game music is rare and this is 20MB of it in ninja-adventure alone; or (b) add per-folder exclusions for musics/, music/ and sounds/ to land at roughly 20MB. I recommend (a) only if the team accepts the growth; otherwise (b). Either way this is the strongest 2D art item in the batch. There are ~35 named contributors and each top-level directory is one author (delapouite, lorc, willdabeast, faithtoken, skoll, ...), so attribution must be tracked per icon used. Budget for this bookkeeping before adopting.
resources.rejection_reason: IMPORTANT VERIFICATION NOTE — there is NO LICENSE/LICENSE.md/LICENSE.txt file; only lowercase license.txt on master. Any automated 'does it have a licence' check will report NO LICENCE and wrongly reject this. It is properly licensed. Count claim verified: I counted 4239 .svg files (claim said 4,239 — exact). 22MB clone / 18MB worktree. The only real cost is the per-author attribution obligation, which is why I would not treat these as drop-in placeholder art.

resources.name: PolygonalMind/initiative-opensource-release

Pack sizes: AvatarGarden 1353 MB, 100AvatarsR2 820 MB, 100AvatarsR1 463 MB, AvatarShow 263 MB, AvatarWebcam 156 MB, CryptoAvatarsWorld 144 MB, SouthDCL 132 MB, TombChaser1 82 MB, RetroBooth 71 MB, LowPolyStore 62 MB, ABM 52 MB, TombChaser2 21 MB, MedievalFair 19 MB, MomusPark 17 MB, ChromaticChaosVHS 10 MB, CrystalCrossroads 9 MB, XYZ 8 MB. The sparse list above is ~85 MB. Take a dozen .vrm files, not all 200.
resources.fetch_command:
# DO NOT VENDOR. Index the URL only. If a human later needs one pack, and only then:
# git clone --filter=blob:none --no-checkout --depth 1 --no-tags -b main https://github.com/PolygonalMind/initiative-opensource-release /tmp/pm && git -C /tmp/pm sparse-checkout set --no-cone 'License.md' 'PolygonalMind_OpenSource/2302_CrystalCrossroadsAssetPack/' && git -C /tmp/pm checkout
# then convert FBX->glTF and TIF->PNG offline before anything enters this repo.
resources.rejection_reason: DOWNGRADED TO LINK-ONLY ON TWO INDEPENDENT GROUNDS. (1) SIZE — I measured it: 6130MB working tree, 8372MB with .git. That is 13x our entire current repo, and even performing the clone to verify it cost 8GB of disk. The researcher's proposed sparse set is not small either: the six named environment packs total 81MB and the 100AvatarsR1 *.vrm glob is 173MB (100 .vrm files) — 254MB combined, a 55% increase on a 461MB repo, for art we do not yet know we want in a genre we have not chosen. (2) FORMAT — this is the fatal one and the proposal does not mention it. I enumerated file extensions per pack: MedievalFair is 40 .fbx + 38 .tif, CrystalCrossroads 67 .fbx + 5 .tif, TombChaser2 61 .fbx + 43 .tif, XYZ 60 .fbx. Godot 4 cannot import .fbx without a separately installed FBX2glTF/ufbx converter binary, and it cannot import .tif AT ALL. So the environment packs are not usable assets in this engine — they are a conversion project. The .vrm avatars would additionally require the godot-vrm addon, which is not in our tree and is not in this batch. The pitch ('17 themed environment packs') is accurate about content and wrong about readiness. Record the URL and the CC0 status in the index; let a human pull a single pack and convert it if a 3D direction is actually chosen.

resources.name: TR-808 drum samples (tidalcycles/sounds-tr808-fischer)
resources.license_evidence: main/LICENSE is the full Creative Commons CC0 1.0 Universal legal code.
resources.asset_license_note: Assets are CC0, attribution not required.
resources.why: 116 clean CC0 TR-808 drum hits organised by instrument (bd8 bass drum, sd8 snare, ch8 closed hat, cp8 clap, cy8 cymbal, lt8/ht8 toms, ma8 maracas, cl8 clave) with per-instrument JSON metadata. This is the raw material for building rhythm/beat-synced audio or for assembling loops at build time — the percussion layer that ZzFXM and pyfxr do not give you convincingly.
resources.teaches: Standard drum-kit instrument taxonomy and multi-velocity sample naming (SD0050, SD2550, SD5010 = decay/tone variants).
resources.notes: Files use uppercase .WAV extension, which matters on case-sensitive filesystems and in Godot import paths. Includes a _soundmeta/ folder of 16 JSON descriptors. Small enough to vendor whole.
resources.verified_license: DISPUTED — repo asserts CC0-1.0, but the samples are third-party 1994 freeware with no formal grant from the copyright holder
resources.fetch_command: # REJECTED — do not fetch.
resources.attribution_required: Unresolvable — the copyright holder has granted nothing in writing
resources.rejection_reason: REJECT. This is downstream licence laundering, and it is exactly the failure mode the brief asked me to catch: 'freeware / ABSOLUTELY FREE with no formal licence' re-labelled CC0 by a redistributor who is not the rights holder and who records that fact in his own metadata. A third party cannot dedicate someone else's work to the public domain; the CC0 file in this repo is an assertion the maintainer had no standing to make. Our policy explicitly forbids '"credit appreciated" with no formal licence' and instructs 'Uncertain = reject, not maybe' — this is squarely that. The fact that the TidalCycles sample corpus is widely used in the livecoding community is not a licence. RECOMMENDED SUBSTITUTE that needs no new verification: the already-approved jsfxr (Unlicense) plus ZzFXM (MIT) synthesise percussion from parameters with no provenance question at all, and the CC0 Superpowers packs above contain 250 genuinely CC0 audio files including drums and SFX.

Verified absent, not merely unfetched.
resources.asset_license_note: Irrelevant — no grant covers the code either. Assume all rights reserved.
resources.why: Recorded because it is the closest thing to a canonical GDScript pattern catalogue (221 stars) and an agent will find it and want it. It must NOT be vendored: a public repo with no licence file grants no rights, which is an explicit hard rule here. Listing it with the verified absence of a licence is more useful than silently omitting it, because it stops a future sweep from re-discovering and mis-vendoring it.
resources.teaches: Chapter-by-chapter GDScript implementations of exactly the patterns the brief lists: 04 composition over inheritance, 05 singleton/global state, 06 observer, 07 factory, 08 state, 09 command, 10 strategy AI, 11 decorator, 12 service locator, 13 event queue — each with a 01.start and 02.finished project.
resources.notes: ACTION FOR HUMANS: this is the one repo worth an email to Packt asking them to add the MIT LICENSE they use on their other Godot titles (Godot-4-Best-Practices, Godot-4-Game-Development-Cookbook and Godot-4-for-Beginners are all MIT). If it ever gains a licence, vendor it immediately. Until then, DISTIL the pattern list into our own GDScript notes — pattern structures are ideas, not expression. resources.name: Dot Hop
resources.license: MIT (source code and documentation only; art/sound/music explicitly excluded)

It is the cleanest available example of the last-20% work: a single `GodotSteam.gd` autoload wraps every Steam call so non-Steam builds still run; `Store.gd` + `PuzzleStore.tscn` + `ThemeStore.tscn` split persistence from gameplay; puzzles are authored as plain text grids (`dothop.txt`, `data/`) parsed at runtime rather than as scenes, so content is diffable; `PuzzleAnalyzer` is a solver used as a content-validation pass over authored puzzles (a pattern any level-based game should copy); `Navi` is a scene-router autoload and `Juice`/`DJ`/`Sounds` isolate feel and audio. resources.name: Tanks of Freedom II
resources.license: MIT (code AND most graphical assets); audio is CC BY-SA 4.0 / CC BY 4.0; docs/ marketing media proprietary

Vendoring only scripts/scenes/campaign keeps us clean and drops the repo from 2145 MB to a few MB.
resources.why: Shipped on Steam (app 3071660) and MIT for code and graphics — one of the very few permissively-licensed Godot 4 games that actually released commercially. The architecture is worth copying wholesale: thirteen autoloads all named as *services* and all living in scripts/services/ (MapManager, GamepadAdapter, SimpleAudioLibrary, MouseLayer, SceneSwitcher, MatchSetup, Settings, Campaign, SavesManager, Online, Multiplayer, Autodiscovery, Relay) — a clean answer to 'what belongs in an autoload'. saves_manager.gd is the reference save design: an index file at user://saves.json holding {map,label,turn,save_id,created_at} metadata, with the heavy per-save payload in separate user://save/*.tofsave.json files, plus three reserved autosave slots (IDs 0-2) ahead of user slots — so the load menu renders without deserialising any save. Also carries a built-in map editor (UGC), hot-seat + online play with LAN autodiscovery and a relay fallback, and a gamepad adapter layer.
resources.teaches: A service-oriented autoload layout and a slot-based JSON save system in a Steam-released turn-based strategy game.
resources.notes: github.com/P1X-in/Tanks-of-Freedom-3-D is the same project under an older name (identical project.godot) — index one, not both.

resources.name: A Dark Forest (GodotProjectZero)

TLDR: Code (*.gd files) are licensed under MIT, but assets (shaders, music, art, writing) are licensed under various CC licenses by respective creators." — enumerates e.g. "cracked_glass.gdshader by rupti licensed under CC-BY-NC-SA 3.0" and "[\"Forest Song 1\", ...] by BurkeZerk licensed under CC-BY-NC-SA 4.0"

resources.why: Released on Steam (app 3314970) and on itch, Godot 4.4, MIT code, ~10 contributors, and the save/localisation work is exactly the 'last 20%' we need to learn. global/autoload/ holds Resources, SaveFile, Locale, Audio, SignalBus, Scene — the SaveFile autoload keeps a dictionary of named save_datas, a default_save_data template used to migrate old saves forward, a SIGNATURE constant and .json extension for user-shareable saves (there is a save_file_imported signal and a save-file picker as the game's main scene), and an AUTOSAVE_SECONDS driven from a Game.PARAMS table. Locale is its own autoload backing shipped EN/FR/ZH-Hans/PT-BR translations added post-launch — a concrete example of retrofitting localisation. Content (resources, workers, substances, events, unlocks, tab levels) is plain dictionaries edited through the resources_spreadsheet_view addon, which is a cheap and copyable approach to balance data.
resources.teaches: Named multi-slot JSON saves with autosave and user-facing import/export, plus a localisation pipeline, in a Steam-released idle game.
resources.notes: Same author's TakinGodotTemplate is the extracted, reusable version of this architecture — mention it in the index as the template sibling.

resources.name: Fortune Mill
resources.license_evidence: raw main/LICENSE: "MIT License / Copyright (c) 2026 Fortune Mill"
resources.asset_license_note: MIT is granted repo-wide, but the repo carries 126 MB assets/, 23 MB music/, 19 MB fonts/, 18 MB videos/ and 6 MB sfx/ — fonts in particular are third-party and the blanket MIT may be sloppy rather than deliberate. Vendor code only; do not reuse the art/music/fonts without separate verification.
resources.last_activity: released on Steam 2 June 2026; repo created 2026
resources.why: The freshest data point available: a commercial Steam release (app 4731620, 2 June 2026, by Lavaflame2 of Melvor Idle) whose full source is MIT. Two architectural lessons stand out. First, the autoload list is deliberately tiny and C#-first: GameInitializer.cs plus UpdateCoordinatorNode.cs — a single coordinator that drives per-frame work instead of scattering _Process across hundreds of nodes, which is the right call for an incremental game with thousands of tickable entities. The rest (FontDb, SharedGameResources, MiscGlobals, AudioManager, Settings) are .tscn autoloads, showing the scene-vs-script autoload split. Second, the design itself is a case study in progression: five+ 'rooms' (darts, scratch-offs, dice, sushi, jackpots) each with their own upgrade curve, where every room's upgrades multiply the others — read src/ for how those cross-system synergies are represented without turning into spaghetti.
resources.teaches: A single-tick update coordinator and cross-system synergy/upgrade economy in a C# Godot 4.5 game that shipped on Steam this year.
resources.notes: C# project — needs the .NET-enabled Godot build to open. Good counterweight to the GDScript-only examples in this set.

resources.name: Museum of All Things
resources.license_evidence: raw main/LICENSE: "Copyright 2025 Maya (https://github.com/m4ym4y/) / MIT License"
resources.asset_license_note: Code MIT. addons/ (85 MB) is mostly godot-xr-tools (MIT) — check before redistributing. assets/ is 123 MB. Note the *runtime* content is Wikipedia text/images (CC BY-SA), fetched at play time and never shipped in the repo — that is a licence-architecture lesson in itself, not a contamination of the code.
resources.last_activity: active 2025-2026; featured in the official Godot showcase
resources.why: Shipped free on Steam and itch, MIT, Godot 4.5, and its autoload list is a performance masterclass that directly matches our desktop/Steam-Deck target: DataManager, ExhibitFetcher, GraphicsManager, WorkQueue (ThreadSafeWorkQueue.gd), RequestSync, ItemProcessor, GlobalMenuEvents, SettingsManager, UISoundManager, GridManager, CacheControl, MipmapThread, LanguageManager. Every exhibit room is built at runtime from a Wikipedia article — so the codebase had to solve, in public, the exact problems a procedural or open-world game hits: a thread-safe work queue feeding generation off the main thread, a dedicated mipmap-generation thread so texture uploads don't stall rendering, RequestSync to coalesce in-flight fetches, CacheControl to persist fetched content under user:// between runs, GraphicsManager for quality presets, and GridManager for the procedural room/hallway layout. Threads are available to us and user:// is a real directory, so all of it transfers.
resources.teaches: How to generate and stream 3D content on background threads without frame hitches, and how to cache it to user:// across sessions.
resources.notes: Also ships a VR mode via godot-xr-tools; ignore that path for us, the desktop build is the interesting one.

resources.name: Bread Adventure

The value is the shape of src/global/: Achievement (a plain enum ID list — STORY_START/STORY_SHIP/STORY_END, COLLECT_*, DEFEAT_* — so gameplay code fires a local enum and never touches Steam directly) paired with PlatformManager (the seam where Steam vs non-Steam builds diverge), plus Config, Status, scene_loader, input_manager, ui_manager, sound_manager, game_logger, special_effect. That is a complete, tiny, copyable answer to 'how do I wire achievements without coupling the game to Steamworks'. Because it is Apache-2.0 end-to-end it is the safest full-repo vendor in this set.

resources.notes: Only ~69 stars but far above its weight for our purpose: it is a *shipped* Godot 4.5 metroidvania under a fully permissive licence, which is rare.

resources.name: Microverse

resources.why: A god-simulation sandbox where autonomous agents live, talk and remember — architecturally the interesting parts are GameSaveManager (persisting a live agent population, not just a player profile), MemoryManager (per-agent memory store, the hard part of any sim with persistent NPCs), CharacterManager, DialogManager and SettingsManager, plus SaveLoadUIManager as a .tscn autoload showing the save-UI split. MIT, 37 MB, Godot 4.4. Lower priority than the shipped games above — it has an LLM/APIManager dependency baked into the design that we would not copy — but it is the only permissive Godot 4 example here of persisting a whole simulated population.

resources.name: Escoria demo game
resources.license_evidence: raw main/LICENSE: "Copyright (c) 2012-2020 Juan Linietsky, Ariel Manzur. / Permission is hereby granted, free of charge, ... without restriction ..." (verbatim MIT text)
resources.asset_license_note: MIT at root covering the demo; game/ (21 MB) art is part of the demo grant. addons/ (12 MB) is escoria-core itself, MIT.
resources.why: Fills the one genre nothing else in our library covers: classic point-and-click adventure. It is a complete playable game that doubles as the reference implementation for the Escoria framework, on Godot 4.6, MIT, and only 52 MB. The architecture is deliberately unlike everything else here — a *single* autoload (escoria) fronting the whole framework, with game logic authored in the ESC event language rather than GDScript, plus a saves/ directory showing the serialised world-state format (room states, item states, global flags). Even if we never build an adventure game, the 'author content in a small DSL, keep the engine generic' pattern is the transferable lesson, and it is the cheapest way for the team to prototype a narrative genre.
resources.teaches: A domain-specific scripting language (ESC) for rooms, items and events, and how to persist a whole adventure world's state.
resources.notes: Note we already vendor godot-open-rpg (which bundles Dialogic) — Escoria is the adventure-game counterpart, not a duplicate.

resources.name: Reia
resources.license_evidence: raw master/LICENSE: "GNU AFFERO GENERAL PUBLIC LICENSE / Version 3, 19 November 2007"
resources.asset_license_note: AGPL-3 throughout. Zero reuse.
resources.why: One of the larger in-development Godot 4 action-RPG codebases, notable for pairing the Godot client with a Rust backend and for supporting single-player, multiplayer and MMO modes from one client. AGPL-3 makes it strictly LINK-ONLY — AGPL's network clause is the most dangerous licence in this list for a commercial product, so it must never be cloned into third_party/.
resources.teaches: Splitting a Godot 4 client from a Rust server while keeping a playable offline mode.
resources.notes: Netcode specifics are the parallel sweep's territory; keep this entry for the architecture-lesson tag only.

resources.name: OpenLiberty
resources.license_evidence: raw main/LICENCE: "MIT License / Copyright (c) 2023 JeanKouss"
resources.asset_license_note: MIT code; ships no copyrighted game assets (the player supplies their own GTA III data). screenshots/ is 12 MB and can be dropped.
resources.why: An open-world Godot 4.3 project whose entire architecture is three autoloads — GameManager, MapBuilder, AssetLoader — because the world is not authored in the editor at all: AssetLoader parses external GTA III-era model/texture archives at runtime and MapBuilder assembles the world from map definition files, with a mods/ directory layered on top. That is the pattern for any game whose content is too large or too data-driven to live as .tscn files, and the streaming/LOD/instance-management code is the part worth reading regardless of what genre we pick. Small (46 MB), MIT, actively developed. Note there are two repos with this name; this (openfw-game) is the maintained Godot 4 one.
resources.teaches: Loading and streaming a large 3D world from external archives at runtime rather than importing everything into the project.
resources.notes: The other repo, FOSS-Supremacy/OpenLiberty, is also MIT ('Copyright (c) 2023 JeanKouss' in LICENCE) and appears to be the earlier/forked lineage — index openfw-game as canonical.

resources.name: OpenCiv3 (C7)
resources.license_evidence: raw master/LICENSE: "MIT License / Copyright (c) OpenCiv3 contributors"
resources.asset_license_note: MIT covers the repo; the game requires the player's own legally-owned Civilization III install for art/data at runtime — no third-party assets are redistributed, which is itself a licensing pattern worth noting.
resources.why: The cleanest example in this sweep of the architecture split every large simulation game eventually needs. The repo is three projects, not one: C7Engine (the rules simulation, plain C#, no Godot types), C7 (the Godot 4.4 presentation project, whose autoloads are just GlobalSingleton and LogManager — deliberately thin), and QueryCiv3 (a parser for the original Civ III data files). That separation makes the simulation unit-testable and headless-runnable, makes saves a property of the engine rather than of the scene tree, and keeps the Godot layer swappable. Only 24 MB, MIT, and actively developed. If the team picks any strategy/simulation genre, this is the structural template.
resources.teaches: Keeping the simulation in a plain C# library that knows nothing about Godot, with Godot as a replaceable view layer.
resources.notes: C# — needs the .NET Godot build. Default branch is `Development`.

resources.name: OpenVic
resources.license_evidence: raw main/LICENSE.md: "MIT License / Copyright (c) 2023 OpenVicProject"
resources.asset_license_note: MIT for the code. Like OpenCiv3 it loads assets from the player's own Victoria II installation rather than redistributing them. The C++ simulation lives in a submodule (openvic-simulation) — a --depth 1 clone without --recurse-submodules gets the Godot side only, which is what we want.
resources.last_activity: active Aug 2026; already on Godot 4.7 (our exact engine line)
resources.why: Runs on Godot 4.7 — the same line we target — and is the reference for the GDExtension route: the openvic-simulation C++ core sits behind extension/, with the Godot project in game/ as the interface layer. Its autoload set reads like a checklist of the platform work we will need: GameSettings, Vic2Settings, ModSettings, WindowOverride, Events, GameLoader (staged/progressive loading of a very large data set with progress reporting, instead of a blocking load), SoundManager, MusicManager, SaveManager, CursorManager, Keychain (input-remapping, the same addon Pixelorama uses) and ControlsGlobal. If we ever need native-speed simulation under a Godot front end, or a serious settings/mod/input layer, this is the place to read.
resources.teaches: Driving a C++ GDExtension simulation from a Godot UI, with a staged GameLoader that keeps the app responsive during heavy startup.
resources.notes: Pair with OpenCiv3 in the index: same problem (big simulation, thin view), two different languages for the core (C++ GDExtension vs C# library).

resources.name: Thrive

resources.why: The biggest and longest-running open-source Godot game that actually sells/ships on Steam, on Godot 4.7 with C#. Worth reading for: its custom ECS layered over Godot nodes (the standard answer when node-per-entity stops scaling), its save system with explicit save-version upgrade paths across years of releases, its mod loader, and its multi-stage structure where a single product contains several distinct game modes (microbe → multicellular → macroscopic) sharing one save and one settings layer. Its CONTRIBUTING/process docs are also a model for a multi-contributor Godot project. STRICTLY LINK-ONLY: GPL-3 is on the forbidden list — read it in a browser, never copy code or clone it into third_party/.
resources.teaches: Running a custom C# ECS and a versioned save format inside Godot, in the largest open Godot 4 game codebase that ships on Steam.
resources.notes: If the team wants an ECS, take the idea from here and the implementation from a permissive library (e.g. an MIT C# ECS), not from Thrive.

LINK-ONLY because it is Godot 3 (config_version=4); the content-pipeline idea transfers, the code does not.
resources.teaches: Managing hundreds of hand-authored levels as data, with tuning curves separated from the puzzle engine.
resources.notes: Good counterexample to 'levels as scenes' for any content-heavy 2D genre.

Also solid physics-object networking. Marked LINK-ONLY purely because it is still on the Godot 3 line (config_version=4) — the code will not port cleanly to 4.7, so read the design, don't vendor the tree.

resources.why: The brief asked for exact sparse-checkout paths for a well-chosen OFL set, and google/fonts is one of the few font sources reachable here (fonts.google.com itself is blocked). 11 MB buys a complete typographic system: UI, wide-language-coverage UI fallback, display, monospace and four distinct pixel faces — enough to style any of the candidate genres without a designer.
resources.teaches: Variable-font axis usage (Inter opsz+wght, Noto Sans wdth+wght, Roboto wdth+wght) — one file replaces a whole weight family, which matters for export size.
resources.notes: Measured: sparse working tree 11 MB, 21 MB including .git; per-family 1-5 MB (notosans 5 MB is the largest). MSDF-friendly: inter, notosans, roboto, spacegrotesk, jetbrainsmono, orbitron, bungee. NOT MSDF-friendly (import as bitmap-crisp, Nearest filter, integer sizes only): silkscreen, pressstart2p, vt323, pixelifysans. Clone recipe: git clone --depth 1 --no-tags --filter=blob:none --sparse https://github.com/google/fonts && git sparse-checkout set <paths>.

resources.name: Atkinson Hyperlegible
resources.license_evidence: raw main/OFL.txt: "Copyright 2020 Braille Institute of America, Inc.\n\nThis Font Software is licensed under the SIL Open Font License, Version 1.1."
resources.asset_license_note: OFL-1.1 — ship OFL.txt with the font, do not sell the font itself, and rename if we modify it.
resources.why: fonts.google.com is blocked; this GitHub source is vendorable and gives us a legitimate 'high-legibility font' option in the accessibility settings menu, which is a cheap, high-impact a11y feature.
resources.teaches: A typeface engineered by the Braille Institute for low-vision readers — disambiguated letterforms (I/l/1, O/0, b/d) that measurably improve character recognition.
resources.notes: Latin + basic Cyrillic/Greek coverage; not a CJK solution.
resources.fetch_command: git clone --filter=blob:none --no-checkout --depth 1 --no-tags -b main https://github.com/googlefonts/atkinson-hyperlegible third_party/atkinson-hyperlegible && git -C third_party/atkinson-hyperlegible sparse-checkout set --no-cone 'fonts/ttf' 'fonts/otf' 'OFL.txt' 'README.md' && git -C third_party/atkinson-hyperlegible checkout
resources.attribution_required: No attribution clause, but the OFL text MUST travel with the fonts — do not vendor fonts/ without OFL.txt.
resources.rejection_reason: CLEAN and the reasoning holds — fonts.google.com is blocked in this sandbox but this GitHub source is fully clonable, so it is a legitimate route to a high-legibility accessibility font. Measured 5MB total. Narrowed the sparse paths from the proposed 'fonts' to fonts/ttf + fonts/otf because fonts/ also contains a webfonts/ subdirectory Godot cannot use. Note this pairs with, rather than duplicates, the ggbotnet CC0 collection: that one is display/pixel flavour, this one is the legibility option for an accessibility settings menu.

resources.name: Noto Sans CJK
resources.license_evidence: raw main/Sans/LICENSE: "This Font Software is licensed under the SIL Open Font License, Version 1.1." (per-directory licence file)
resources.asset_license_note: OFL-1.1 per Sans/LICENSE and Serif/LICENSE — no root LICENSE file, so cite the per-directory file.
resources.why: Godot's built-in font has zero CJK coverage; if we ever translate to zh/ja/ko this repo is the answer. Repo is very large, so index it and pull a single regional OTF plus subset with fontTools rather than vendoring wholesale.
resources.teaches: The reference open CJK family (SC/TC/JP/KR), including single-region subsets and Super-OTC variants.
resources.notes: Alternative: be5invis/Sarasa-Gothic (OFL-1.1, verified: 'This Font Software is licensed under the SIL Open Font License, Version 1.1.') which merges Inter/Source Han for a tighter Latin+CJK UI/mono pairing; its build repo is source-only, take TTFs from Releases.

resources.name: GGBotNet CC0 font collection
resources.license_evidence: curl https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ggbotnet/fonts-cc0/main/LICENSE -> CC0 1.0 Universal text ('...exclusive Copyright and Related Rights (defined below) upon the creator... voluntarily elects to apply CC0 to the Work...'). README: '# GGBotNet Fonts CC0 / License: Please read file LICENSE for details. / Credits: Type designer GGBotNet'.
resources.asset_license_note: CC0 — no attribution required, single author (GGBotNet), so provenance is clean. 38 MB for 143 font files; consider cherry-picking families if size matters.
resources.why: Zero-friction fonts: CC0 rather than OFL, so no licence file has to travel with the export and there are no Reserved Font Name traps — useful when a build pipeline or a jam build needs to stay simple. ~40 families / 143 files with genre flavour that google/fonts lacks: 3x3 Mono and Gridtile (micro pixel), Delta Block and Jupiteroid (sci-fi display), Pixelated Elegance, Home Video and MatrixType (retro/CRT), Crayon Libre and Drybrush (hand-drawn), Braille CC0 and Braille Display (accessibility/novelty), Operation Napalm (military display).
resources.teaches: Nothing pedagogical — this is a pure asset drop; its value is licence simplicity, not technique.
resources.notes: Measured by real clone: 38 MB, 143 .ttf/.otf files. Ships a PREVIEW.png. Quality is hobbyist-good rather than Inter-grade — use for flavour/display, keep google/fonts for body UI text.
resources.fetch_command: git clone --filter=blob:none --no-checkout --depth 1 --no-tags -b main https://github.com/ggbotnet/fonts-cc0 third_party/fonts-cc0 && git -C third_party/fonts-cc0 sparse-checkout set --no-cone 'LICENSE' 'README.md' '*/*.ttf' '*/*.otf' && git -C third_party/fonts-cc0 checkout
resources.rejection_reason: Licence perfect; trim the payload. Measured 38MB working tree, and the composition is: 18.2MB of ttf/otf (143 files, which is the '143 files' the researcher counted), 11.6MB of preview PNG/JPG specimen images, and 4.6MB of woff/woff2 web formats Godot cannot use. Sparse to */*.ttf and */*.otf halves it to ~18MB with zero loss of capability. Counted 46 font families (not the claimed ~40); the named families all check out (3x3 Mono, Gridtile, Delta Block, Jupiteroid, Pixelated Elegance, Home Video, MatrixType, Crayon Libre, Drybrush, Braille CC0, Braille Display, Operation Napalm, plus Public Pixel).

resources.name: Inter
resources.license_evidence: raw master/LICENSE.txt: "Copyright (c) 2016 The Inter Project Authors ... This Font Software is licensed under the SIL Open Font License, Version 1.1."
resources.asset_license_note: OFL-1.1 — ship LICENSE.txt with the font.

resources.teaches: A UI-optimised variable font with Latin + Greek + Cyrillic coverage, tabular figures, and optical sizing — the safe default for menus/HUD text at small sizes.
