resources.name: Dialogue Manager (nathanhoad)
resources.license_evidence: raw .../main/LICENSE -> 'MIT License\n\nCopyright (c) 2022-present Nathan Hoad and Dialogue Manager contributors.'; README line 60: 'Licensed under the MIT license'
resources.asset_license_note: Code only; no third-party art or audio bundled.
resources.why: The text-file counterpart to Dialogic's visual editor, and the ONLY item in this sweep already targeting Godot 4.7 — which matches this repo's engine version exactly. Text-based dialogue diffs cleanly in git and is far easier for a coding agent to generate than Dialogic's editor-authored resources; that is a real advantage given the index is built for agents.
resources.teaches: Nonlinear dialogue as a plain-text markup language with its own parser: titles/jumps, inline conditions and mutations that call back into GDScript, tags, translation extraction, and a C#-friendly runtime.
resources.notes: Carry BOTH this and Dialogic — they suit different workflows (writer-with-GUI vs agent/programmer-with-text). Best thing to steal: the dialogue-file grammar and its mutation syntax for calling game code mid-line.
resources.fetch_command: git clone --depth 1 --no-tags -b main https://github.com/nathanhoad/godot_dialogue_manager third_party/godot_dialogue_manager
resources.rejection_reason: CLEAN and the claim checks out: config/features=PackedStringArray("4.7", "C#") — genuinely the only item in this batch already on 4.7, matching our engine. plugin.cfg version 3.10.1. Repo also carries v1.x/v2.x/v3.x maintenance branches; clone main. Includes a .csproj/.sln for the optional C# bindings — harmless for a GDScript project.

resources.name: BulletUpHell
resources.license_evidence: clone of branch Demo-V4.4 -> LICENSE.md 'MIT License\n\nCopyright (c) 2024 Dark Peace'
resources.asset_license_note: Repo on the Demo-V4.4 branch is addon code only — no bundled art or audio, so no asset licence to track.
resources.godot_version: Godot 4 (branch Demo-V4.4; plugin.cfg version="4.4"); separate V3.x branches exist for Godot 3
resources.why: The 'hundreds of entities' requirement is the hard part of the survivors-like/bullet-heaven genre, and this is the most feature-complete permissive answer in the Godot ecosystem. At 1MB it is nearly free to keep, and it also serves twin-stick and boss-fight needs in other genres.
resources.teaches: How to run thousands of bullets without thousands of nodes: pooled/shared bullet representation, resource-driven spawn patterns (rings, spirals, arcs, custom curves), trigger-based pattern chaining, and per-bullet behaviour modifiers driven from the Inspector.
resources.notes: IMPORTANT: clone with `-b Demo-V4.4` — the default resolution picks up 'Alpha' which has no LICENSE.md. README states V4.3 is 'the final free version' and future updates move to a paid 'BLAST' version; the MIT grant on what is published is irrevocable, but do not expect upstream to keep improving. Best thing to steal: the Resource-based pattern definitions (spawn pattern as data, not code).
resources.fetch_command: git clone --depth 1 --no-tags -b V4.3 https://github.com/Dark-Peace/BulletUpHell third_party/BulletUpHell
resources.rejection_reason: BRANCH CORRECTION — the researcher did not specify a branch and there is NO 'main'/'master'. HEAD points to 'Demo-V4.4'. The repo README states verbatim: 'Yes. But the V4.3 is the final free version. The next update will be part of the premium BLAST version.' Demo-V4.4 is therefore the demo branch of a commercial product; although its LICENSE.md is also MIT and I found no crippling code (grep for demo/watermark/premium/trial in addons/*.gd returned nothing), the safe, unambiguously-free target is branch V4.3, whose LICENSE.md I fetched and read: 'MIT License / Copyright (c) 2023 Dark Peace'. Pin V4.3. No project.godot (pure addon), README documents Godot 3 and 4; plugin.cfg version 4.3/4.4.

resources.name: Dialogic
resources.license_evidence: raw .../main/LICENSE -> 'MIT License\n\nCopyright (c) 2020 - present Emilio Coppola'; README line 80: 'Dialogic may use the Roboto font, licensed under Apache license, Version 2.0'
resources.asset_license_note: Both licences are permissive. Apache-2.0 (Roboto) is on our allowed code list and is fine for fonts; record it in attribution if shipped.
resources.why: By far the highest-leverage narrative tool in Godot and directly enables the visual-novel/narrative genre outright — but it also serves RPG, adventure and even strategy briefings, so it holds value under almost any genre the team lands on. The in-editor timeline means writers can work without touching code.
resources.teaches: A complete narrative stack with an in-editor timeline authoring UI: branching dialogue with conditions and variables, character/portrait management with expressions, styled text boxes and layered backgrounds, choice handling, glossary, and save-anywhere via its own state system.
resources.notes: Best thing to steal even if unused wholesale: the Timeline-as-Resource format, which makes dialogue diffable and lets non-programmers author content.

resources.name: netfox
resources.license_evidence: raw.githubusercontent.com/foxssake/netfox/main/LICENSE -> "Copyright 2023 Gálffy Tamás / Permission is hereby granted, free of charge, to any person obtaining a copy of this software and associated documentation files (the \"Software\"), to deal in the Software without restriction..." (verbatim MIT body). No non-free art: examples use primitives and CC0-style placeholder meshes.
resources.asset_license_note: Code MIT. Example art is simple geometry/primitives authored in-repo; no third-party art packs bundled. Fonts/icons are netfox's own branding (part of the MIT repo).
resources.godot_version: Godot 4.x (README: "Godot 4.x is supported by netfox"); addon v1.48.4; examples written against 4.1 and open fine in 4.x
resources.why: THE default answer for Godot 4 real-time netcode in 2026. Actively maintained (commits this month), MIT, pure GDScript so no build step, and the only mature option that gives you tick sync + client-side prediction + server reconciliation + rollback + interpolation in one package. Ships four addons (netfox, netfox.noray, netfox.extras, netfox.internals) plus nohub.gd (lobby client), trimsock.gd and vest (test lib). Crucially for an undecided team, it is genre-agnostic: the examples cover an FPS, a 3D brawler (Forest Brawl, a complete shippable game), rollback NPCs, state machines, input prediction and visibility filtering. Vendor the whole repo — the 13 MB of examples is the most valuable part.
resources.teaches: How to layer deterministic tick loops, input serialization, rollback and CSP/SSR on top of Godot's MultiplayerAPI. examples/ contains 15 runnable projects including multiplayer-simple (naive RPC) vs multiplayer-netfox (same game done right) — the single best A/B for understanding why naive RPC feels bad.
resources.notes: DECISION NOTE: netfox is the right default unless your game is a 2-8 player deterministic fighting/action game needing frame-perfect rollback with no server (see godot-rollback-netcode). netfox assumes a client-server topology with one authority; it does NOT make your simulation deterministic for you. Also bundles the noray client, so it pairs directly with the noray server below for NAT punch-through. Free public noray instance at tomfol.io:8890 for prototyping only — do not ship against it.
resources.fetch_command: git clone --depth 1 --no-tags -b main https://github.com/foxssake/netfox third_party/netfox
resources.rejection_reason: APPROVED WHOLE — the researcher's 'the 13MB of examples is the most valuable part' is correct and I measured it (examples/ = 13MB, docs/ = 5MB, addons/ = 2MB, total 20MB). All four netfox addons are at plugin.cfg version 1.48.4 and nohub.gd at 0.9.0, so this really is actively maintained. ONE CORRECTION TO THE PITCH: the repo's project.godot declares config/features=PackedStringArray("4.1"), and the README says plainly 'Forest Brawl and the other examples are written against Godot 4.1. They may or [may not run on newer]'. The ADDONS support Godot 4.x generally ('Godot 4.x is supported by netfox'), but do not promise the team that the Forest Brawl example opens clean in 4.7 — it is a 4.1 project. Also note addons/vest is a test framework, which brushes against the parallel sweep's testing-tooling scope; it is small and part of netfox's own CI, so leaving it is fine.

resources.name: Gaea — node-graph procedural generation framework
resources.license_evidence: raw.githubusercontent.com/gaea-godot/gaea/main/LICENSE -> 'MIT License / Copyright (c) 2023 BenjaTK'
resources.asset_license_note: Demo art in demos/ is small and covered by the repo MIT; no third-party art bundled.
resources.godot_version: 4.7 (project.godot config/features=PackedStringArray("4.7", "Forward Plus")); default branch 2.0. v1.X branch for Godot <=4.3
resources.why: Best single breadth bet in this domain. A visual graph of generators + modifiers covering caves, terrain, walkers and noise, output to 2D tilemaps or 3D gridmaps, with custom nodes easy to author. Matches our exact engine version (4.7) and is the fastest path from 'we picked a genre' to 'we have a world'.
resources.teaches: Composable procgen: cellular automata, walker/random-walk, heightmap/noise, modifier stacks, wired together in a visual graph and emitted to TileMapLayer or GridMap.
resources.notes: README self-describes 2.0 as 'early development, may not yet be optimized for larger, more complex projects' — good for prototyping and jams, verify perf before shipping a large world. BenjaTK/Gaea is the author's fork/mirror and also carries branches named 4.6 and 4.7.
resources.fetch_command: git clone --filter=blob:none --no-checkout --depth 1 --no-tags https://github.com/gaea-godot/gaea third_party/gaea && cd third_party/gaea && git sparse-checkout set --no-cone 'addons/gaea' 'script_templates' 'LICENSE' 'README.md' && git checkout

It does not: project.godot declares config/features=PackedStringArray("4.3", "Forward Plus"). It is still Godot 4 and will open in 4.7, but correct the index metadata to 4.3 or an agent will trust a wrong compatibility signal. Licence and everything else verified. Clone 8MB / 7MB worktree; addons/gaea is 2MB (testing/ is 5MB, excluded).

resources.name: MikeSchulze/gdUnit4 (now godot-gdunit-labs/gdUnit4)
resources.license_evidence: raw master/LICENSE: 'MIT License / Copyright (c) 2023-2026 Mike Schulze' (identical at MikeSchulze/gdUnit4, same HEAD sha 4586b80)
resources.asset_license_note: code only for the addon subtree; the 25 MB assets/ dir is banners/screenshots, excluded by the sparse checkout
resources.godot_version: 4.3 - 4.7.1 (README badges list v4.7 and v4.7.1); addon version 6.2.1
resources.why: RECOMMENDED FRAMEWORK. Ran it live on Godot 4.7.1 headless: 2 tests, 1 deliberate failure, exit 100, auto-produced reports/report_1/results.xml (JUnit) and index.html with zero config, and reported '0 orphans'. Already present at 6.1.3 inside third_party/beehave, so adoption cost is near zero and avoids two competing test frameworks. Has a first-party GitHub Action.
resources.teaches: Fluent assertion style, scene runners, orphan/leak accounting, and how a test framework reports into CI.
resources.notes: CI FOOTGUNS I HIT: runtest.sh does NOT pass --headless itself (X11/Wayland failure), and gdUnit4 hard-refuses headless with exit 103 unless you add --ignoreHeadlessMode. Working command: GODOT_BIN=/path/to/godot ./addons/gdUnit4/runtest.sh --headless --ignoreHeadlessMode --add res://test. Full clone is 66 MB but 25 MB is assets/ and 8 MB documentation/; addons/gdUnit4 alone is 5 MB.

resources.name: Deckbuilder Framework (insideout-andrew)
resources.license_evidence: raw .../main/LICENSE -> 'MIT License\n\nCopyright (c) 2024 insideout-andrew'
resources.asset_license_note: Repo-wide MIT; bundled playing-card art is part of the MIT-licensed repo with no third-party carve-out.
resources.why: The rules-side complement to Simple Card Pile UI from the same author, on a newer engine target (4.3). Ships a standard 52-card deck so a traditional card game is playable immediately, while the signal API keeps it usable for a Slay-the-Spire-style deckbuilder.
resources.teaches: Card and deck mechanics as data plus signals: shuffling, drawing, dealing, deck/discard cycling, and a signal-per-event API ('connect the signals decks emit and use them to make your game') so effect resolution stays in your code rather than in the framework.
resources.notes: Best thing to steal: the signal-driven boundary — the framework never decides what a card *does*, only when it moves.

resources.name: godot-hexgrid (jeremyz)
resources.license_evidence: raw .../master/LICENSE.md -> 'Copyright (c) 2020, Jérémy Zurcher / Permission is hereby granted, free of charge, to any person obtaining a copy of this software and associated documentation files (the "Software"), to deal in the Software without restriction...' (verbatim MIT text)

resources.name: Rhythm Game Utilities
resources.license_evidence: raw .../main/LICENSE -> 'The MIT License (MIT)\n\nCopyright (c) 2026 Scott Doxey'; README line 1614: '[The MIT License (MIT)](./LICENSE)'
resources.asset_license_note: Code only; no bundled music (which matters — most rhythm repos bundle copyrighted songs).
resources.godot_version: Godot 4 via bindings (engine-agnostic core; also targets Unity, Unreal, SDL, MonoGame)
resources.why: Chart formats and tempo maps are the second hard problem in rhythm games, and this is the only permissive library that solves them with an explicit Godot target. Together with RhythmNotifier it makes the rhythm genre genuinely startable rather than merely possible.
resources.teaches: The data side of rhythm games that RhythmNotifier does not cover: parsing chart formats (.chart, and a StepMania parser in progress), tick<->second conversion, BPM/tempo maps with changes mid-song, and note-hit windows.

resources.verified_license: MIT ('The MIT License (MIT) / Copyright (c) 2026 Scott Doxey')
resources.fetch_command: git clone --filter=blob:none --no-checkout --depth 1 --no-tags https://github.com/rhythm-game-utilities/rhythm-game-utilities third_party/rhythm-game-utilities && cd third_party/rhythm-game-utilities && git sparse-checkout set --no-cone 'GodotPlugin' 'RhythmGameUtilities' 'include' 'Makefile' 'LICENSE' 'README.md' && git checkout

It is a C++ library requiring a compile step, not a drop-in GDScript addon; the README support matrix lists Godot 4 (GDScript and C#, macOS/Windows/WebGL) as Tested ✅ but Stable ❌ on EVERY row, including Unity and Unreal. Godot tested at 4.3, not 4.7. Sparse set drops the 5MB UnityPackage from the 12MB/11MB clone. Treat as experimental, not production-ready.

resources.name: Zylann/godot_voxel
resources.license_evidence: LICENSE.md, master: "MIT License / Copyright (c) 2016-2024 Marc Gilleron / Permission is hereby granted, free of charge, to any person obtaining a copy of this software and associated documentation files (the \"Software\"), to deal in the Software without restriction"
resources.asset_license_note: MIT code. Being an engine module rather than a GDExtension addon, it imposes a custom Godot build on the whole team — a real cost to weigh before adopting.
resources.godot_version: Godot 4.x C++ engine module (branches 1.1, 1.2); requires a custom engine build or a matching prebuilt
resources.why: The heaviest-duty procedural-content generator available to us: fully generated, editable, infinite 3D worlds with zero downloaded geometry. Only worth pulling if the team lands on survival/sandbox/mining, which is why it is link-only rather than vendored — but it is the highest-ceiling option in the 'generate instead of download' category and should be one hop away in the index. Note the already-vendored Terrain3D covers heightmap terrain; this covers volumetric.
resources.teaches: Voxel terrain architecture: chunked streaming, LOD transitions, smooth (transvoxel) versus blocky meshing — the standard reference implementation in the Godot ecosystem.
resources.notes: Do not vendor speculatively. Record in the index as 'the answer if the genre becomes voxel/survival/destructible'.

resources.name: Colyseus (authoritative room server)
resources.license_evidence: raw.githubusercontent.com/colyseus/colyseus/master/LICENSE -> "Copyright (c) 2015-2026 Endel Dreyer / MIT License:"
resources.asset_license_note: Code MIT. No art.
resources.godot_version: n/a — engine-agnostic Node/TypeScript server; Godot 4 client story is the weak link (see notes)
resources.why: The best MIT, self-hostable alternative to Nakama when you do not need accounts/persistence, only authoritative rooms. Its delta-encoded schema sync over WebSocket is an excellent fit for a card game, a board/strategy game or any browser game, and it sidesteps the whole NAT/UDP problem because WebSocket works everywhere including web export. Tiny (5 MB) and updated this month.
resources.teaches: Room-based authoritative multiplayer: schema-based delta state sync over WebSocket, room lifecycle (onCreate/onJoin/onMessage/onLeave), matchmaking by room filter — a much lighter mental model than Nakama for turn-based games.
resources.notes: DECISION NOTE — the Godot client is the catch. gsioteam/godot-colyseus (MIT) is Godot 3 only (project.godot config_version=4) and dead since Sept 2023; colyseus/native-sdk (MIT, C) is early and only started Oct 2025; colyseus-unity-sdk (MIT, C#) works from Godot with the .NET build. If you are GDScript-only, you will either write a thin WebSocket+JSON client yourself or pick Nakama instead, which has a first-party maintained GDScript SDK. Index Colyseus as 'read before choosing', vendor because it is cheap.
resources.fetch_command: git clone --depth 1 --no-tags -b master https://github.com/colyseus/colyseus third_party/colyseus
resources.rejection_reason: Licence clean throughout the monorepo. Default branch is 'master', not 'main'. Measured 4MB (the claimed 5MB was the with-.git figure). CAVEAT ON FIT: this is the SERVER only — there is no Godot client in this repo. resources.notes: Godot 3 only and the port would be significant work. Index as the reference design for 'if we pick a 2D platformer with smart enemies'.

resources.name: godot-multiplayer (thegatesbrowser) — client-server template with VOIP
resources.license_evidence: raw.githubusercontent.com/thegatesbrowser/godot-multiplayer/main/LICENSE -> "MIT License / Copyright (c) 2024 Nordup Ondar"
resources.asset_license_note: Code MIT. Art is Kenney Platformer Kit 2.2, credited in README as CC0 — clean. The addons/twovoip binaries are of UNVERIFIED licence: exclude them.
resources.why: The highest-star (250) modern Godot 4.5 multiplayer template on GitHub, MIT, and the only permissively licensed one that ships working voice chat. Voice is a feature teams universally underestimate and it is genre-independent — it makes a co-op roguelite, a 3D shooter or a social game viable without a second integration project.
resources.teaches: An end-to-end wiring of Godot's built-in MultiplayerAPI (MultiplayerSpawner + MultiplayerSynchronizer) with player identity, menus, and real-time Opus voice chat — the last of which almost no other template has.
resources.notes: SIZE WARNING: measured 170 MB, of which 141 MB is addons/twovoip (prebuilt Opus/GDExtension binaries for every platform). Sparse-vendor everything EXCEPT addons/twovoip and add twovoip back from its own upstream release when you actually need voice — otherwise you carry 141 MB of binaries you cannot audit. NOTE: I could not locate twovoip's upstream repo or licence from this sandbox (the obvious GitHub path 404s) — treat those binaries as UNVERIFIED and do not ship them until a human confirms the licence.
resources.fetch_command: git clone --filter=blob:none --no-checkout --depth 1 --no-tags -b main https://github.com/thegatesbrowser/godot-multiplayer third_party/godot-multiplayer && git -C third_party/godot-multiplayer sparse-checkout set --no-cone 'main/' 'player/' 'ui/' 'voip/' 'user_data/' 'levels/' 'defaults/' 'project.godot' 'README.md' 'LICENSE' 'addons/kenney_platformer_kit/' && git -C third_party/godot-multiplayer checkout
resources.attribution_required: No, but the MIT notices for BOTH Nordup Ondar and GDQuest must be preserved (add player/LICENSE to the sparse list).
resources.rejection_reason: THE HEADLINE CLAIM DOES NOT SURVIVE THE SPARSE SET. Measured full tree 150MB, and 141MB of that is addons/twovoip — a GDExtension shipping PREBUILT BINARIES for every platform (macOS universal debug+release .dylib at 12MB each, Linux .so 8MB each, Android arm32/arm64/x86_32/x86_64 debug+release, iOS, Windows .dll, and four Web .wasm variants). The researcher's own sparse list EXCLUDES addons/twovoip while the justification is 'the only permissively licensed one that ships working voice chat'. Both cannot be true: voip/ is four GDScript files (microphone.gd, voip_manager.gd, voip_user.gd, voip_user.tscn) that call into the twovoip GDExtension, so with twovoip excluded the voice feature is non-functional code. Decide deliberately: (a) vendor as listed and index it as 'voice chat REFERENCE — requires installing two-voip-godot-4 separately', or (b) accept +141MB of opaque prebuilt binaries, which I do not recommend for a repo already at 461MB and which additionally carry NO licence file in-tree (the MIT claim for twovoip is a README credit, not a licence text I could verify inside this repository). I have written (a) into the sparse list, and ADDED player/LICENSE-bearing player/ plus levels/ and defaults/ which the original list omitted but project.godot references. config/features=PackedStringArray("4.5", "Forward Plus") — the 4.5 claim is correct.

resources.name: godot-3d-multiplayer-template (devmoreir4)
resources.license_evidence: raw.githubusercontent.com/devmoreir4/godot-3d-multiplayer-template/main/LICENSE -> "MIT License / Copyright (c) 2024 Carlos Armando Moreira"
resources.asset_license_note: Code MIT. README Credits section names 3D-Godot-Robot-Platformer-Character as CC0 — clean, and the only third-party art. 27 MB of assets/ (characters, fonts, items); verify the fonts folder licence before shipping.
resources.godot_version: project.godot config/features=PackedStringArray("4.6", "Forward Plus") — the most current Godot version of any template found
resources.why: The best 'what does current best practice look like with NO third-party netcode addon' reference, on Godot 4.6, actively maintained into mid-2026, MIT, with clean CC0 art. Vendoring this alongside netfox gives an agent the plain-MultiplayerAPI baseline and the prediction-enabled version side by side, which is exactly the comparison a team needs before committing to a netcode stack.
resources.teaches: Vanilla Godot 4.6 high-level multiplayer done cleanly — MultiplayerSpawner/MultiplayerSynchronizer, host-vs-join flow — plus a run_headless_server.sh showing the `godot --headless --path .` dedicated-server pattern.
resources.notes: DECISION NOTE: built-in MultiplayerAPI with no prediction is genuinely sufficient for co-op, turn-based, party, and slow-paced games at 2-8 players — most teams reach for rollback when they did not need it. Start here, measure, and only add netfox when the feel demands it. The headless server script is the concrete answer to 'how do I run a dedicated server' (export with the dedicated-server/headless preset, no rendering, no audio).
resources.fetch_command: git clone --filter=blob:none --no-checkout --depth 1 --no-tags https://github.com/devmoreir4/godot-3d-multiplayer-template third_party/godot-3d-multiplayer-template && cd third_party/godot-3d-multiplayer-template && git sparse-checkout set --no-cone 'scripts' 'scenes' 'project.godot' 'run_headless_server.sh' 'LICENSE' 'README.md' && git checkout
resources.attribution_required: unknown for the art, which is precisely the problem; none for the MIT code
resources.rejection_reason: DOWNGRADED from full vendor to code-only sparse. The stated value is the netcode reference ('what best practice looks like with NO third-party addon'), which lives entirely in scripts/ and scenes/ — 2MB. The 27MB assets/ tree is unverified provenance and contributes nothing to that argument, so excluding it removes the only real risk at no cost to the rationale. Godot 4.6 confirmed. Full clone 50MB / 29MB worktree.

resources.name: godot-3d-multiplayer-template (BatteryAcid) — netfox + noray reference
resources.license_evidence: raw.githubusercontent.com/BatteryAcid/godot-3d-multiplayer-template/master/LICENSE -> "MIT License / Copyright (c) 2024 BatteryAcidDev"
resources.asset_license_note: CODE MIT — VERIFIED. ART UNVERIFIED: asssets/ contains characterLargeMale.fbx and militaryMaleA.png (they look like Kenney Blocky Characters, CC0) but the repo states NO asset licence and has no credits section. Per our policy that is not good enough — exclude asssets/ from any vendoring and do not ship that art.
resources.godot_version: project.godot config/features=PackedStringArray("4.3", "Forward Plus"); README: "Godot Version: 4.3 (Should work in 4.4)", Netfox 1.19.1 (netfox is now 1.48.x — expect API drift)
resources.why: Small (13 MB) and it is the missing glue between three things we would otherwise have as separate parts — netfox, noray, and a real 3D character controller. Animation state synchronization under rollback is a genuinely hard problem most templates dodge; this one solves it with RewindableStateMachine, which is worth vendoring for that alone.
resources.teaches: The exact integration an agent otherwise has to derive: netfox + noray P2P + netfox.extras RewindableStateMachine driving a 3D character's Idle/Walk/Run/Jump/Fall states with synchronized animation, and a host-or-dedicated-server switch.
resources.notes: DECISION NOTE: pinned to netfox 1.19.1 on Godot 4.3 and untouched since April 2025 — read it as a pattern reference, then re-implement against current netfox rather than running it as-is. ASSET RISK: see asset note; sparse-vendor code only.

resources.name: Yet Another Roguelike Tutorial in Godot (SelinaDev)
resources.license_evidence: raw.githubusercontent.com/SelinaDev/Godot-Roguelike-Tutorial/main/LICENSE -> 'MIT License / Copyright (c) 2023 Selina'
resources.asset_license_note: Bundled tileset/font assets are covered by the repo-wide MIT declaration; no separate asset licence file, so treat art as MIT-granted by the author but prefer replacing it for a shipped game.
resources.why: The single most complete free Godot roguelike infrastructure reference — FOV, turn scheduling and RNG in idiomatic GDScript, with each chapter a runnable project so an agent can diff part_N against part_N+1 to isolate exactly the code that implements one system.
resources.teaches: The full roguelike spine, one commit-sized chapter at a time: procedural dungeon, FOV/shadowcasting, turn-based scheduling, entity actions, AI, inventory, save/load.
resources.notes: 118 MB full clone because it stores 13 complete copies of the project (part_1..part_13). Sparse-vendor part_12 (the near-final state) plus part_4 (the FOV chapter) and you are under 30 MB. Godot 4.1 project — opens in 4.7 with minor deprecation warnings.
resources.fetch_command: git clone --filter=blob:none --no-checkout --depth 1 --no-tags -b main https://github.com/SelinaDev/Godot-Roguelike-Tutorial third_party/Godot-Roguelike-Tutorial && git -C third_party/Godot-Roguelike-Tutorial sparse-checkout set --no-cone 'part_4' 'part_12' 'LICENSE' 'README.md' && git -C third_party/Godot-Roguelike-Tutorial checkout
resources.rejection_reason: SPARSE IS ESSENTIAL AND THE PROPOSAL GOT IT RIGHT. Measured full tree 116MB because the repo is 14 COMPLETE COPIES of the same project (part_0 … part_13, each 6–16MB, each with its own duplicated Kenney assets). The proposed part_4 + part_12 subset measures 22MB — verified. ONE CAVEAT ON THE PITCH: the 'diff part_N against part_N+1 to isolate one system' workflow is real, but it only works if you take consecutive parts; part_4 and part_12 are eight chapters apart, so their diff is not a single feature. If diffability is the actual goal, take a consecutive pair as well. ENGINE AGE: part_12 declares config/features=PackedStringArray("4.2") and part_4 declares "4.1" — this is a 4.1/4.2-era tutorial, older than statico's 4.6 roguelike. Index both, but point agents at statico's src/ for current idiom and at SelinaDev for the step-by-step derivation.

resources.name: Konado

resources.license_evidence: raw .../main/LICENSE -> 'The MIT License (MIT) Copyright (c) 2023-present, DSOE1024 ... GodotHub'; README line 120: '**MIT License**: [LICENSE-MIT](./LICENSE)'; clone -> assets/Assets_License.txt: 'The project mascot Kona and the banners are licensed under the CC-NC-SA 4.0 license.'; addons/konado/fonts/ResourceHanRoundedCN-OFL-License.txt

resources.why: The only VN kit found that gives you templates and surrounding systems (achievements, settings) rather than just a dialogue engine, and it is on Godot 4.7. Strong CJK/font support is a differentiator if localisation ever matters.

resources.fetch_command: git clone --filter=blob:none --no-checkout --depth 1 --no-tags https://github.com/godothub/konado third_party/konado && cd third_party/konado && git sparse-checkout set --no-cone 'addons/konado' 'addons/konado_settings' 'addons/konado_achievement' 'LICENSE' && git checkout

All three claimed addon dirs verified present. Sparse subset measures 36MB, but 29MB of that is CJK fonts under addons/konado/fonts — if CJK/localisation is not a near-term need, add ':(exclude)addons/konado/fonts' and the footprint drops to ~7MB. Godot 4.7, matches our engine exactly.

The autoload list shows the composition strategy: third-party addons (Pandora for typed game-data entities, InputHelper, SoundManager, phantom-camera, MetSys) sit next to house autoloads (Debug, Navi scene router, DJ, Music, Sounds, Juice, Records, Dino). Reading how Dot Hop and dino share the 'bones' addon is the concrete lesson in what to put in a house framework versus what stays per-game.
resources.teaches: How one developer factors a shared core ("bones") out of several games so the second and third game start at 60%.
resources.notes: Same author as Dot Hop; index the two together — dino is the framework story, Dot Hop is the shipped story.

resources.rejection_reason: SPARSE LIST REWRITTEN — the proposed one is far too big. Measured full tree 1341MB (2289MB with .git). I measured every proposed model directory: the researcher's 23-folder list totals 333MB, because each model directory ships up to four redundant encodings (glTF, glTF-Binary, glTF-Draco, glTF-Quantized) plus screenshots — e.g. FlightHelmet 47MB, Corset 39MB, BarramundiFish 36MB, AntiqueCamera 34MB, BoomBox 31MB, Avocado 31MB, WaterBottle 26MB. Adding 333MB to a 461MB repo is not defensible for a conformance suite. My list keeps every small rig/animation/interpolation test whole (SimpleSkin 3MB, InterpolationTest 1MB, AnimatedMorphCube 1MB, BoxVertexColors 1MB, Cameras 1MB, Suzanne 2MB, TextureCoordinateTest 1MB, CompareMetallic/Roughness/Normal 1MB each) and narrows the heavy PBR props to a single glTF-Binary variant each (WaterBottle 9MB, ToyCar 6MB, NormalTangentTest 2MB) plus FlightHelmet's glTF (it has no -Binary variant). Total ~40MB. DROPPED as pure texture weight with no unique diagnostic value: Lantern, BoomBox, AntiqueCamera, Corset, Avocado, BarramundiFish, CompareBaseColor, CompareAmbientOcclusion, CompareAlphaCoverage — add any of them back individually as glTF-Binary if a specific need appears. Also: the researcher's own claim that 7 models are NON-FREE is confirmed by the LICENSES/ directory contents, which is precisely why a wholesale vendor is forbidden here.

resources.name: nakama-project-template (authoritative server modules + docker-compose)
resources.license_evidence: raw.githubusercontent.com/heroiclabs/nakama-project-template/master/LICENSE -> "Apache License / Version 2.0, January 2004"
resources.asset_license_note: Code Apache-2.0. Includes a vendor/ Go dependency tree — those deps carry their own (permissive) licences. No art.
resources.godot_version: n/a (server-side; pairs with any Nakama client incl. nakama-godot)
resources.why: This is the 'read this before choosing' artefact for server-authoritative design, and it is only 5 MB. Seeing the same authoritative tic-tac-toe match loop in Go, TypeScript and Lua side by side is the fastest way for an agent or a human to understand what 'the server owns the truth' actually costs in code. The docker-compose gets a real backend running locally in one command, which de-risks the whole 'do we even want a backend' question before the genre is picked.
resources.teaches: A complete authoritative match handler written three ways (match_handler.go / match_handler.ts / .lua) — match_init, match_join_attempt, match_loop tick, match_terminate — plus server-side RPCs, daily rewards, and a docker-compose bringing up Nakama + CockroachDB locally.
resources.notes: DECISION NOTE: server-authoritative logic is the ONLY real anti-cheat available to an indie team — validate moves server-side and never trust a client-reported score, position or currency. Client-side anti-cheat (EAC/BattlEye) is priced and operationally scoped for studios, not indies; do not plan around it. Contains no Godot client — pair with nakama-godot.

resources.name: Steering behaviors for Godot 4 (konbel)
resources.license_evidence: raw.githubusercontent.com/konbel/steering-behaviors-godot-4/main/LICENSE -> 'MIT License / Copyright (c) 2024 SomeLazyGuy'

resources.why: Godot 4 has no built-in steering framework and GDQuest's well-known steering toolkit is Godot 3 only. This is a small, MIT, current-engine reference for the movement layer that sits under almost any enemy AI — and unlike a boids demo it separates the individual behaviours so you can lift one.
resources.teaches: Reynolds steering primitives in idiomatic Godot 4 GDScript: seek, flee, arrive, wander, obstacle avoidance, and the group behaviours (separation, cohesion, alignment) that compose into flocking.
resources.notes: Author frames it as a learning project — treat as adaptable reference code rather than a drop-in addon.

resources.why: This is the 'how do I actually build a theme' answer. Pair it with a theme-type/variation naming convention and it becomes our design system starting point regardless of genre.
resources.teaches: A base Theme that reproduces Godot's default look for every Control type, so you restyle by editing an existing complete theme instead of discovering the ~40 theme properties one broken node at a time.
resources.notes: Theme type variations (e.g. a 'DangerButton' variation) are the mechanism to prefer over per-node theme overrides.

resources.name: Godot 4 Roguelike Tutorial (Bozar)

resources.license_evidence: raw.githubusercontent.com/aikoncwd/Godot-FOV-algorithms-roguelike/main/LICENSE -> 'MIT License / Copyright (c) 2023 AikonCWD'
resources.asset_license_note: Small tileset, repo-MIT.
resources.godot_version: Godot 3.x (algorithms are pure GDScript, port is trivial)
resources.why: 1 MB, MIT, and it isolates line-of-sight from everything else. Comparing two implementations in one project is more useful to an agent than a single opinionated one buried in a roguelike tutorial.

This looks like a Godot 3 project despite the 2023 copyright. The brief says to downgrade anything Godot-3-only. It is 1MB of readable line-of-sight algorithm, so vendoring it as an ALGORITHM REFERENCE is still defensible, but do NOT index it as a runnable Godot 4 project, and note that the parallel statico/godot-roguelike-example vendor (Godot 4.6, src/) already gives us a working FOV implementation — which undercuts the 'FOV has no other permissive Godot 4 reference' justification used for that item.

resources.teaches: The canonical WFC algorithm from its author: overlapping vs simple-tiled models, entropy/propagation/backtracking, and the sample/tileset data formats every port copies.

resources.name: ValveSoftware/GameNetworkingSockets
resources.license_evidence: raw.githubusercontent.com/ValveSoftware/GameNetworkingSockets/master/LICENSE -> "Copyright (c) 2018, Valve Corporation / All rights reserved. / Redistribution and use in source and binary forms, with or without modification," (3-clause BSD)
resources.asset_license_note: Code BSD-3-Clause. No assets.
resources.godot_version: n/a — C++ transport library; this is the open-source core of ISteamNetworkingSockets
resources.why: Reference-grade. When someone asks 'why not just use UDP directly' or 'what is ENet missing', this is the answer with source you can read. BSD-3 so it is even usable directly if you ever write a custom GDExtension transport, and it is exactly what SteamMultiplayerPeer sits on top of.
resources.teaches: What a production UDP game transport actually provides beyond raw sockets: reliable+unreliable channels on one connection, message fragmentation/reassembly, bandwidth estimation, encryption, and connection state machines. Its docs are the clearest free explanation of the Steam Datagram Relay model.
resources.notes: Read-before-choosing, not vendor. In practice Godot's built-in ENetMultiplayerPeer already gives you reliable/unreliable channels and is the right default; this exists to explain the tradeoffs and to be the fallback if you need Valve's relay outside Steam.

resources.name: noray (NAT punch-through + relay server)
resources.license_evidence: raw.githubusercontent.com/foxssake/noray/main/LICENSE -> "Copyright 2023 Gálffy Tamás / Permission is hereby granted, free of charge, to any person obtaining a copy of this software and associated documentation files (the \"Software\"), to deal in..." (MIT body).
resources.asset_license_note: Code MIT. No assets.
resources.godot_version: Engine-agnostic Node/Bun service; the Godot side is the netfox.noray addon
resources.last_activity: 2026-08-03 ("fix(relay): Don't exit when a UDP reply bounces (#84)")
resources.why: The problem that kills more indie multiplayer games than netcode does is that neither player can accept an inbound connection. noray is a tiny (1 MB), MIT, self-hostable Node service that does host registration, NAT hole punching and relay fallback, and it has first-class Godot support because netfox ships the client addon. Ships a Dockerfile and docker-compose. Actively maintained alongside netfox.
resources.teaches: Why 'it works on LAN but not over the internet' happens, and the standard fix: registration + external-address discovery + UDP hole punching, with a relay fallback when punching fails.
resources.notes: DECISION NOTE: only needed for peer-hosted/P2P topologies. If you go authoritative-dedicated-server, players connect out to your server and NAT traversal is a non-issue — skip noray entirely. Relay mode costs you bandwidth, so budget for it if you ship P2P.
resources.fetch_command: git clone --depth 1 --no-tags -b main https://github.com/foxssake/noray third_party/noray
resources.rejection_reason: CLEAN, and the claims verify: 1MB, Dockerfile and docker-compose.yaml both present at root, src/ + bin/ + test/ + scripts/. Same author and licence as netfox, and netfox already ships the addons/netfox.noray client, so the pairing is real rather than aspirational. Uses bun.lock as well as package.json — running it needs Node/Bun and an npm install, which is fine (registry.npmjs.org is reachable). Not a Godot addon; index it under 'service you self-host', not 'addon'.

Runtime modules can be Go plugins, TypeScript or Lua. Postgres/CockroachDB required. Measured 78 MB at --depth 1; do not vendor.

resources.name: Ultimate Retro Shader Collection (PSX/N64/Saturn 3D look)
resources.license_evidence: main/LICENSE.md: 'MIT License / Copyright (c) 2024-2025 Zorochase'

It converts the CC0 low-poly kits above into a deliberate aesthetic rather than a compromise. Does not overlap the parallel sweep's 2D neon/glow work.
resources.teaches: How 5th-gen console artefacts are actually produced — vertex snapping in the vertex shader, affine UVs by disabling perspective correction, ordered dithering as a screen-reading pass — and by extension how to give a 3D game a strong look on a tiny art budget.
resources.notes: Alternatives verified: MenacingMecha/godot-psx-style-demo (MIT, 'Copyright (c) 2020 MenacingMecha', the original reference implementation) and scolastico/psx_visuals_gd4 (MIT, 'Copyright 2026 Joschua Becker', packaged as a plugin). URSC is the broadest and the only one confirmed on 4.7.

resources.rejection_reason: CLEAN and every claim verified. Does not overlap the parallel sweep's 2D neon/glow work — this is 3D vertex-snapping/affine-mapping/3-point-filtering.

It is a single screen-space shader, which is about as version-resilient as Godot code gets, so the risk is low — but 'works over 2D or 3D' is the author's claim, not something I could execute here.

resources.name: ShaderFunction-Extras
resources.license_evidence: raw.githubusercontent.com/paddy-exe/ShaderFunction-Extras/main/LICENSE.md -> 'MIT License / Copyright (c) 2023 Patrick Exner (FlameLizard)'

This is that library — noise, SDF, easing, colour-space and remap helpers as includable .gdshaderinc files. 1 MB, MIT, and it multiplies the value of every other shader we vendor.
resources.teaches: Idiomatic use of .gdshaderinc as a shared function library — the mechanism that lets hand-written shaders stop duplicating noise/SDF/easing helpers.

resources.name: GDQuest godot-shaders

The demo's source code (script files, scene files, shaders, and generally all Godot-generated resources) is available under the MIT license. 2. resources.name: godot4-cel-shader

Highest-optionality pick for any stylised 3D direction, and it composes with the already-vendored Kenney 3D starter kits.
resources.teaches: A complete non-photoreal pipeline rather than one shader: banded lighting, rim/specular control, per-object and post-process outlines, and how to keep them consistent across many materials.

resources.name: GodotSSRWater

resources.why: The only 3D water candidate found that is current with Godot 4.7 and small (2 MB). Fills a real hole: the repo's only water is Terrain3D's ocean plane and the compute water_plane demo. Solves the specific problem that Godot's built-in SSR does not apply to transparent materials, which is exactly what water needs.
resources.teaches: Hand-rolled screen-space reflection inside a spatial shader, plus depth-buffer-driven fake refraction and transparency — the two things Godot's built-in SSR will not do on a transparent surface.

resources.name: gamedevserj Godot-Shaders

MIT, Godot 4.2, no asset-licence complication.
resources.teaches: Compact single-file 2D effects with clearly named uniforms — easy for an agent to lift one shader without dragging in a framework.

resources.name: AcerolaFX-Godot

Technically this is one of the most attractive things in the domain — a Godot port of Acerola's well-known FX suite, brand new (July 2026), from the author of the 957-star Acerola-Compute. But there is no licence file of any kind, and a public repo with no licence grants no rights. Flagging it explicitly so nobody re-finds it and assumes MIT by association with the author's other repos. Same author's Godot-PSX (191 stars) has the identical problem.

resources.name: GodotRetro
resources.license_evidence: raw.githubusercontent.com/ahopness/GodotRetro/4.x/LICENSE -> 'Creative Commons Legal Code / CC0 1.0 Universal'
resources.why: Single highest-value drop in this domain. CC0 (no attribution burden at all), tracking Godot 4.7 exactly, and it closes three separate gaps at once: CRT (basic + complex), VHS, VHS-pause, TV, glitch (simple + complex), film grain (simple + complex), lens distortion, posterization, dithering, monochrome, sharpness, blur, colour correction and PSX lit/unlit. Critically it is also the ONLY vendored source of CompositorEffect examples — the repo currently has zero, and CompositorEffect is how post-processing is actually done in Godot 4.
resources.teaches: How to write a Godot 4 CompositorEffect: each effect ships twice, once as a canvas_item .gdshader and once as a compute .glsl driven from GDScript, so the pair is a side-by-side lesson in porting a screen shader to the compositor pipeline.

resources.name: OpenGamepadUI
resources.license_evidence: raw main/LICENSE: "GNU GENERAL PUBLIC LICENSE / Version 3, 29 June 2007"

Even for a game, the 'every control reachable by d-pad, nothing assumes a mouse' problem is exactly what Deck certification checks. GPL-3, so LINK-ONLY — read the patterns, do not copy the code.
resources.teaches: Controller-first UI focus handling and Linux/Steam-Deck input plumbing, at production quality, in Godot 4.7.
resources.notes: Highest-value link-only entry for the Steam Deck side of our target.

resources.name: Pixelorama
resources.kind: shipped Godot 4 desktop app (not a game)
resources.license_evidence: raw master/LICENSE: "MIT License / Copyright (c) 2019-present Orama Interactive and contributors"
resources.asset_license_note: MIT across code and the bundled UI assets; check individual palettes/fonts before redistributing.
resources.why: Not a game, but the most complete example we can legally read of a Godot 4.7 product that actually ships on Steam, and it is only 18 MB. Translations/ carries a .pot plus ~40 .po locales (af_ZA, ar_SA, be_BY, bg_BG, ca_ES, cs_CZ, cy_GB, da_DK, ...) — the reference for a real localisation pipeline. The autoloads are the checklist: Global, Import, OpenSave (a versioned custom project format with backwards compatibility), DrawingAlgos, Tools, Export, Palettes, Keychain (user-rebindable input, reusable as-is), ExtensionsApi (a first-class plugin/mod API with a stability contract), Themes (runtime theming), Preferences. There is also an installer/ directory and release CI. When our team hits settings menus, keybinds, translations, save-format migration or mod support, this is the one-hop answer.
resources.teaches: Every non-gameplay system a Steam-released Godot 4 product needs: i18n, preferences, keybinds, themes, a versioned file format and a plugin API.
resources.notes: Tag it clearly as 'app, not game' in the index so genre queries don't surface it, but 'how do I do X for release' queries do. Sibling shipped Godot 4.7 apps with the same lessons and the same MIT terms, verified but not separately vendored: Material Maker (raw master/LICENSE.md '# MIT License ... Copyright (c) 2018-present Rodolphe Suescun'), GodSVG (raw main/LICENSE 'MIT License / Copyright (c) 2023 MewPurPur'), Lorien (raw main/LICENSE 'MIT License / Copyright (c) 2021-2025 Marcus Brummer').

resources.name: GDQuest godot-4-stylized-sky

resources.why: A stylised (non-photoreal) sky, which Sky3D deliberately is not. Small, one focused sky shader, and it is the counterpart to the realistic option so the team can pick an art direction later without re-searching.

resources.name: godot-toon-outline

It complements Terrain3D's already-vendored grass particle shader, which handles ground cover but not tree canopies.
resources.teaches: Vertex-displacement wind sway with per-instance phase offset and correct two-sided normals for alpha-cut leaf cards.
resources.notes: Godot 4.0-era; expect minor 4.7 syntax touch-ups. See domain_notes: the CC0-claiming Malidos grass repo had to be rejected for having no LICENSE file.

resources.name: tree-and-foliage-wind-shader-godot

resources.name: Malidos Grass-Shader-Example
resources.license: NONE — README claims CC0 but there is no licence file
resources.license_evidence: Checked LICENSE, LICENSE.md, LICENSE.txt, COPYING, LICENCE on main and master: all 404. README.md contains only the line 'CC0 MultiMesh Grass Shader for Godot' — a topic tag and a title, not a licence grant.
resources.why: REJECTED ON LICENCE, and worth recording because it looks safe at a glance: the repo carries a 'cc0-license' GitHub topic and its README's only line asserts CC0, but no licence document exists. Under our hard rule a repo with no LICENSE file grants no rights, and a one-line README title is not a formal grant. This is exactly the 'credit appreciated with no formal grant' failure mode. MultiMesh grass remains an unfilled gap because of it.

resources.name: Takin Godot Template
resources.license_evidence: raw master/LICENSE: "MIT License / Copyright (c) 2024 TinyTakinTeller"
resources.why: Read it as a worked example rather than a dependency. It is the most complete permissive demonstration of a multi-slot save file system plus localisation plus options menus actually integrated, and its addon selection is itself a curated recommendation (debug_menu, logger, resonate, resources_spreadsheet_view, scene_manager, script-ide) — two of which this sweep independently arrived at. Maaack's template (already vendored) covers menus and persistence better; Takin's value is the save-slot and localisation wiring Maaack's leaves thinner.

resources.name: godot-ci (abarichello)

resources.teaches: The actual mechanic of the -col/-onlycol convention: on export it duplicates selected objects, suffixes the duplicate so Godot's importer generates a separate collider, then deletes the duplicate so your Blender outliner stays clean. That trick is the whole art of the Blender→Godot handoff.
resources.notes: Last commit 2024-10; the glTF suffix conventions it automates are stable engine behaviour, so age matters less here than for gameplay code. Pair it with the written conventions in my domain_notes (suffixes -col/-convcol/-colonly/-navmesh/-occ, 1 unit = 1m, apply transforms, prefer .glb or direct .blend import over FBX).

resources.name: jsfxr (chr15m)

Zero runtime dependencies (no npm install), so it works offline forever once vendored. Genre-agnostic: every game type needs coin/hit/jump/select/explosion sounds. Params.toB58() encodes a whole sound as one short text string, so sounds can live in git as text and be re-rendered deterministically.

The bundled sfxr-to-wav CLI works but triggers a Node 22 Buffer() deprecation warning. Presets: pickupCoin, laserShoot, explosion, powerUp, hitHurt, jump, blipSelect, tone, click, random.

Note the repo advertises a paid 'jsfxr pro' (jsfxr-pro-screenshot.png) but the open repo itself is unambiguously Unlicense — unlike BulletUpHell, there is no crippled-demo branch problem here.

Uniquely it also does musical synthesis — pyfxr.tone('E4') and pyfxr.pluck(duration=1.0, pitch='A4') produce real notes, so it can generate melodic/UI-chime material as well as SFX.

resources.name: ZzFX

resources.why: The best candidate for RUNTIME sound generation rather than build-time. Its entire synth is ~100 lines of plain arithmetic over 20 parameters — no dependencies, no file format — which makes it the one generator here that can realistically be ported to GDScript so the game synthesises sounds on the fly with zero .wav files shipped. TESTED WORKING headless in Node with a small shim (4 WAVs written). Much wider design space than sfxr's fixed presets.

Stub AudioContext and capture the buffer in createBuffer().getChannelData().set() — that is all it takes; verified. Ships ZzFX.js (full), ZzFXMicro.js (tiny) and a wav.js helper.
